Selling fast in New Rochelle

New Rochelle is a Westchester County city on Long Island Sound, about 17 miles from Midtown Manhattan. Two houses a few blocks apart can feel like different towns: one near the downtown train hub, another on a leafy single-family street, a third on the water at Davenport Neck. That spread is why pricing and condition vary so much from listing to listing.

Population is 85,864, up 7.7 percent from 2020. More than 11,500 single-family houses stand in the city, next to a downtown of condominiums and apartment buildings. There are 31,684 households, and owners occupy only 53.7 percent of housing units, so close to half of residents rent. The typical owner-occupied home is valued at $702,500 and median gross rent is $1,917. If you own a two-family or have a tenant in place, that renter share is your market.

Older houses and what inspectors find

The older streets lean Queen Anne, Tudor Revival and Colonial Revival, and the southwest corner has brownstones, townhomes and red-brick apartment buildings. A house from the first building boom may carry decades of alterations. Old wiring, original windows or an enclosed porch built without a permit are the items a buyer's inspector tends to report.

Access to Manhattan is the strongest selling point. Metro-North's New Haven Line and Amtrak both use the downtown station, and Interstate 95 has four exits inside the city. Lead with the commute when a listing sits near the station.

Property tax bills and the assessment calendar

Expect four bills a year, so a mid-cycle closing has to apportion each of them. City taxes are due by January 31 for the calendar year, county taxes by June 30, and the school and library tax is split into a September 30 half and a March 31 half. Anything paid after the last day of the collection month picks up interest and penalties.

There has been no citywide revaluation since 1956. Instead, each addition or renovation is judged as of December 1 and shows up on the following February roll. A buyer of a freshly renovated house may therefore face a higher bill than you paid.

Recording the deed

The Westchester County Clerk, not City Hall, handles the recording. Ownership records cannot be edited at the city level, so the deed goes to the county through an attorney.

The clerk will take a deed only with paperwork generated in its PREP online system:

  • A recording and endorsement cover page
  • Form TP-584, the state transfer tax return
  • Form RP-5217, the Real Property Transfer Report
  • A payment cover page covering fees and tax

The state levies $2 per $500 of consideration, rounded up to the next $500, and by default that tax is the seller's. A 1 percent mansion tax applies to residences at $1 million and up and falls on the buyer. Your closing attorney can confirm the totals for your deed.

Permits and occupancy paperwork

Unclosed permits and gaps in occupancy paperwork are the usual trouble spots. Building permits are a New York State requirement, and the city takes applications through an online system. No permit is needed to paint outside the Historical district, to resurface a one or two-family driveway without widening it, or to lay siding over existing wall surfaces without replacing the sheathing.

If an earlier owner finished a deck, attic or basement and never closed the permit, the buyer's attorney will want the paper trail. A cash buyer taking the house as-is can accept those gaps, though the offer will reflect them. Call the city's building permit office about your address before accepting any bid.

STAR and what happens at closing

If you receive the STAR credit, close that registration with the state once the sale is done. The buyer registers through the Homeowner Benefit Portal when the house becomes their primary residence.

For the sale itself, gather the deed, tax bills for all four collections, the payoff letter and permit records. At the table you sign the deed and the transfer tax forms, the lender is paid off, and each tax bill is split by the closing date. A cash purchase skips the appraisal and lender conditions, which is where many financed sales of older houses slow down.

How a sale works step by step

Most New Rochelle sales follow the same path. You choose a route, either a listing with an agent or a direct sale to a cash buyer. Once you accept an offer, a buyer's attorney requests the contract, a title search is ordered, and the deed is drafted. A financed buyer adds an appraisal, an inspection and lender conditions, and each one is a chance for the price to be reopened. A cash buyer removes those conditions, so the date on the calendar depends mainly on the title work.

Plan on a few small errands before the closing day arrives. Ask the building permit office for any open applications on your address. Confirm the exact balance on each of the four tax collections. Locate your STAR paperwork if you receive the credit. Have your payoff letter current, since lenders issue figures that are good only for a short stretch.

Pricing an older house without a renovation

Owners of an older house often ask whether it is worth fixing before selling. In a city where the typical owner-occupied home is valued at $702,500, buyers are paying for the location near the train and the water, and many will accept a dated kitchen or bathroom if the price reflects it. Repairs that a lender or inspector will flag, such as old wiring, an unpermitted porch enclosure or an unclosed deck permit, are the ones worth sorting out or disclosing. Everything else can be left to the buyer.

Keep a simple list of repairs with rough costs as you talk to buyers. Compare offers by what you keep after repairs, carrying costs and closing costs, and not only by the headline number. A lower cash offer that closes on your schedule can beat a higher one that needs three rounds of repair negotiation.

If the house has tenants

With close to half of New Rochelle residents renting, a tenant in place is common, especially in two-family houses. A tenant does not stop a sale. A cash buyer can often take the house with the tenant staying, while a buyer who needs a mortgage may want it vacant at closing. Gather the lease and your rent records early, and tell every serious buyer about the arrangement up front so the offer already reflects it.

Which four bills does a New Rochelle homeowner receive?

The city, Westchester County, and the school and library taxes in two halves. City taxes are due January 31, county taxes June 30, and the school halves September 30 and March 31.

Does an open building permit block a New Rochelle sale?

It does not stop a sale, but the buyer inherits the problem, so expect a lower bid or a request to close it first. Ask the city's building permit office which applications are open on your address.

What date is Grievance Day in New Rochelle?

The third Tuesday in February, following the February 1 tentative roll. Exemption forms are due December 1, and the final roll is set April 1.

Which office records a New Rochelle deed?

The Westchester County Clerk, using cover pages and forms created in the PREP system. City staff cannot change ownership records, so the deed and the TP-584 go to the county.

Has New Rochelle revalued every home recently?

No. There has been no citywide reassessment since 1956, and improvements are reviewed one at a time as of December 1.

Sellers here owe a city transfer tax on top of the state one, so judge every offer by what you keep after both. The city also leans hard on building records, and that shapes how smoothly a financed sale closes.

Permit records at the Department of Buildings reach back to the late 1880s, and lenders and title companies pull them before a closing. An open permit or a missing certificate of occupancy can hold up anyone financing the purchase. A cash buyer can simply accept the house as it stands.

Pull together the deed, a payoff statement, recent tax bills and any rental or occupancy papers. That folder answers most early questions from buyers and title agents.

Housing and who owns it

This is a crowded city: 72,304 people on 4.39 square miles, with just 42.9 percent of homes owner-occupied. The typical owner-occupied home is valued at $484,000. Rent is about $1,629 and household income is $78,779.

With most homes rented, a lot of sellers own a two- or three-family building, or inherited one. Those buildings bring occupancy inspections, tenant paperwork and sometimes a vacancy inspection. Cash buyers can often step into a tenanted building instead of waiting for it to empty.

City transfer tax

The city charges 1.5 percent on whatever part of the price is over $50,000, and the grantor, meaning you, pays it. Chapter 234 of the city code sets a 30 day window running from delivery of the deed, and payment must come before recording. New York's state tax of $2 per $500 comes on top.

Both parties swear to a joint return filed with the City Comptroller, whether or not tax is due. A late payment adds an 8 percent penalty and 1.5 percent interest per month. If the seller is exempt, the buyer is stuck with the bill. Check that the closing statement lists the amount, and have your attorney run the numbers on your real price before you accept an offer.

Department of Buildings and certificates of occupancy

The Department of Buildings works from City Hall, 1 Roosevelt Square, Room 210. It issues permits, inspects work and handles certificates of occupancy. The city says a certificate is needed only when major work or a change in use has happened since the house was built.

To see what the city has on record, bring your block and lot number and read the file. If there is no certificate, you apply for one, and missing floor plans must be replaced by plans drawn to architectural standards. Permitted work that departs from the city's records has to be legalized with a new building permit.

  • A permit costs $80 plus $6 per $1,000 of estimated cost, and it stays valid for a year while insurance is current.
  • Roofs may hold two layers at most before all must come off.
  • Fences can reach four feet in front yards on mapped streets and six feet at the sides and rear.
  • Rental units face a vacancy inspection, and large multiple dwellings can face a building-wide task force inspection.

Work without a permit produces a violation and penalty fees. The owner carries the responsibility for permits even if a contractor files them.

Property tax due dates

Assessment roll, grievances and STAR

The Assessor prepares the roll, records every deed transfer and applies exemptions. Look for the tentative roll by June 1. Grievances go to the Board of Assessment Review on the third Tuesday in June, 4 to 8 pm, and the final roll is set August 1. File a separate RP-524 for each parcel; only one grievance per property is allowed.

STAR works a little differently from what many owners expect. Anyone who applied from May 1, 2015 onward registers with the state at tax.ny.gov/star and gets a credit check rather than an exemption.

Recording the deed with Westchester County

Recording happens at the Westchester County Clerk's Land Records Division, which also takes the state TP-584. For fee math, the clerk sends filers to its online Property Records Electronic Portal. Taxes may be paid by ACH, certified check, bank check, attorney escrow check or an approved vendor's check.

The state's return is due by the 15th day after the deed is delivered. The city code wants proof of payment affixed to the deed before it is recorded, so have your lawyer or title agent confirm that the Comptroller has been paid first.

Selling a tenanted or multifamily building

Two- and three-family houses are common in this city, and a tenant does not have to leave for you to sell. A cash buyer can purchase the building with tenants in place and take over the leases. A buyer using a mortgage will usually want vacancy or a clean inspection history first, and that can add weeks.

Gather the leases, rent roll and any inspection reports before you list. If the city has flagged the building for a vacancy inspection or a task force review, resolve or disclose that early. Buyers price in the unknown, and a clear file tends to bring a firmer offer.

Visit the Department of Buildings with your block and lot number and ask what the file shows for your address. Learning about an old open permit in week one is far better than hearing about it from a title agent the day before closing.

What to bring to City Hall

A short trip to the Department of Buildings can answer most questions before a buyer asks them. Bring photo identification, your block and lot number, and any old permits or plans you have stored. Ask for the file on your address, check for open permits, and ask what is needed to close any that remain. If a floor plan is missing, budget for a drawn replacement. Bring notes on what the clerk tells you, then share them with your attorney.

You pick the closing dateClose in as little as 7 days or on the date that works for you, with no fees or commissions.Get My Cash Offer →

From offer to closing

Once you accept an offer, the title company orders a search and reviews the city's building file. If a certificate of occupancy is missing, a financed buyer may ask you to obtain one, which is why many owners of older buildings lean toward cash offers. Meanwhile your attorney prepares the deed, the transfer tax returns and the payoff request. On the closing date you sign, the city and state taxes are paid from your proceeds, and the deed goes to the county clerk for recording.

Frequently asked questions

Does Mount Vernon charge its own transfer tax?

Yes. The city takes 1.5 percent of the price above $50,000, and the seller pays within 30 days of delivering the deed, before recording. New York's $2 per $500 is charged on top.

Who files the joint transfer tax return in Mount Vernon?

Buyer and seller swear to it together, and it goes to the City Comptroller even when no tax is due. Your attorney or title agent usually handles the filing.

Can I sell in Mount Vernon with no certificate of occupancy?

A bank and title company will usually inspect the city's building file for a financed buyer. The Department of Buildings says a certificate is needed only after major work or a change of use. A cash buyer may take the property as-is.

What are the city and county tax due dates?

City tax is due January 31 and July 31. County tax is due April 30.

Where can I see my property's assessment?

The Assessor keeps the roll, and tentative and final versions are posted on the city website. The tentative roll is out by June 1 and becomes final on August 1.

Which part of Southampton is your house in?

Southampton is a large town at the eastern end of Suffolk County, wrapped by the Atlantic Ocean on its south side and Peconic Bay on the north. It covers 293.46 square miles, but only 139.13 of those are land. English settlers from Lynn, Massachusetts founded it in 1640, and the area is widely known as the Hamptons. The town keeps an online map of more than 100 historic markers and districts, which is worth a look if your house is an old one.

The town is a collection of smaller places, and the one on your deed matters more than the town name. Seven incorporated villages sit inside it: North Haven, Quogue, Sag Harbor (partly), Sagaponack, Southampton, Westhampton Beach and West Hampton Dunes. The unincorporated hamlets include Bridgehampton, East Quogue, Flanders, Hampton Bays, North Sea, Noyack, Remsenburg, Riverside, Shinnecock Hills, Speonk, Tuckahoe and Water Mill. A house in an incorporated village may answer to the village's own code office as well as the town.

Housing market and price points

Southampton is expensive, and many of its houses are lived in by owners who plan to stay. The typical owner-occupied value is $928,100, with 82.4% of homes owner-occupied and 90.8% of residents in the same house a year earlier. Gross rent is typically $2,363 a month.

  • Population on July 1, 2025: 71,601, up 3.7% from the 2020 base.
  • Households: 26,576, averaging 2.55 people.
  • Typical household income: $128,594.

A value near $928,100 sits just under the $1 million line that triggers New York's extra mansion tax, so the exact sale price can change what the buyer owes at the closing table. Price your house with that threshold in mind.

Coastal weather and an older house

With about 49.8 inches of precipitation and 26.8 inches of snow a year, about 114 days of measurable precipitation and a shoreline on two sides, moisture is a fact of life for houses here. Keep receipts for roof, siding, drainage and mechanical work, and gather repair paperwork after any storm damage so a buyer's inspector can see what was done and when.

A cash buyer will often take a weathered house as it stands, without asking you to finish the work first, which matters if you do not want to manage contractors through a coastal winter.

Free, no-obligation offerTell us about your Southampton house and get a written cash offer within 24 hours.Get My Cash Offer →

Selling a house that has been rented

You can, but the town's rental permit rules shape how you sell it. Any dwelling rented for any period needs a rental permit, and the Town Code sets a minimum stay of 14 days. Shorter stays count as transient rentals, which the code does not allow. There is no maximum stay.

Southampton rental permit rules
QuestionTown answer
Is a permit needed?Yes, for any home rented for any period
Minimum stay14 days
How long is a permit good?Two years
Does it transfer to a new owner?No, a new owner needs a new permit
Processing timeAbout 1 to 3 weeks, 2 to 4 in summer
Where are applications dropped off?27 Ponquogue Ave., Hampton Bays

Because permits do not pass to a buyer, an investor purchasing a rental has to apply in their own name, and moving a property into an LLC, trust or estate also requires a new permit. Advertising a house for rent without a permit can bring violations, suspension or revocation, and a two-year ban on renting.

There are two routes to a permit. A Standard application is inspected by a New York State certified code enforcement officer from the town's Department of Public Safety. A Certified application uses an architect or engineer the owner hires, and expedited processing is also offered. An owner of a single-family house may rent up to two bedrooms to no more than two renters without a permit, as long as the owner lives there and everyone shares the kitchen and living space.

Property tax dates, penalties and exemptions

Bills leave the Town Receiver of Taxes by December 15. The first half is due January 10 and the second May 31. You can pay at the counter, online, or by mail if the postmark is on or before the due date. An online e-check costs $1.75, and cards carry a 2.5% processor fee.

Paying late hurts. Money sent after January 10 still reaches the Receiver, but 1% interest builds every month. Once May 31 passes, a 5% penalty and 5% interest are added and the town stops taking payment, so the balance moves to the Suffolk County Treasurer's Office in Riverhead, 631-852-3000.

  • Exemption applications, including STAR and the senior and disability exemptions, are due March 1.
  • Grievance Day is the third Tuesday in May, and the Assessor's Office at 116 Hampton Road can help at 631-283-6020.
  • Property details and amounts due are searchable on the town's eTax portal by address, owner's last name, tax map number or bill number, and a duplicate bill can be requested there.
  • Unpaid taxes do not sit forever: the county typically starts collection on vacant land after one year and on improved property after three.

Each side is credited or charged at closing for its share of the tax year, so get current balances before you sign the contract.

Transfer taxes and recording forms

Sellers here owe the state transfer tax, and buyers owe a local charge. The state rate is $2 for each $500 of price, paid by the seller. A buyer owes the 1% mansion tax only on residential prices of $1 million or more.

The town also runs the Community Preservation Fund, which is financed by a two percent real estate transfer tax paid by the purchaser, not the seller. At recording, the county clerk requires a Peconic Bay Region Community Preservation form with every recording in the five East End towns, which are Riverhead, Southampton, East Hampton, Shelter Island and Southold. Both parties sign it.

The Suffolk County Clerk in Riverhead files the deed along with the RP-5217 transfer report and the TP-584 return. Your attorney supplies the deed form, since the clerk sells none, and each party must show a street address, never a P.O. box.

Sell as-isNo repairs, no cleaning and no showings. We buy Southampton houses in any condition.See My Cash Offer →

Steps from offer to closing

First decide who your likely buyer is and what stays with the house. A rented property needs its permit status confirmed, and the buyer should hear early that the permit does not follow the sale. Print your current tax bill from the eTax portal to see what is paid, and set aside repair receipts.

Next your attorney drafts the deed, listing a street address for each party, and sends it with the TP-584, RP-5217 and Community Preservation forms to the clerk in Riverhead. At the closing table the tax year is divided by date between you and the buyer, and state transfer tax is deducted from your proceeds. Cash deals have no lender appraisal or approval to wait on, so you can usually pick the day.

Frequently asked questions

Do I need a rental permit to sell a house I rented out?

A permit is not required to sell, but it is required to rent. Permits last two years and cannot be passed to a buyer, so the new owner applies for their own.

How much interest is added if taxes are late?

After January 10, first-half taxes accrue 1% interest per month. After May 31 a 5% penalty and 5% interest apply, and the balance is collected by the Suffolk County Treasurer.

Who pays the Community Preservation Fund fee?

The buyer pays it. The clerk still requires the Peconic Bay Region form, signed by both parties, with the recording.

Can I rent my Southampton house for a weekend?

Not under the town code. The minimum rental stay is 14 days, and anything shorter counts as a transient rental that is not allowed.

When is the deadline for tax exemptions?

March 1 for exemption filings, including STAR and the senior and disability exemptions. Applications go to the Assessor's Office.

Your selling options in Tonawanda

This page covers the town in Erie County that wraps around the Village of Kenmore, sometimes called Ken-Ton. The city of the same name sits north along the canal and is a different municipality, so confirm which one holds your parcel before you begin. Owners usually weigh an ordinary listing against an all-cash purchase by a direct buyer.

Listing fits a house in show condition when you can sit through a mortgage approval. A direct sale fits when repairs have piled up, a job is moving you out of the area, or an estate has several heirs to coordinate. Compare the net from each path, since the easy route and the profitable route are sometimes different.

  • Agent listing: the most exposure, plus staging, showings and a closing tied to the buyer's bank.
  • Do-it-yourself sale: you price it, host the visits and negotiate the contract.
  • All-cash purchase: no bank involved, with the house accepted as you leave it.

Each path hits one local requirement, a storm water certificate, which is explained further down.

Owning a home in Tonawanda

Tonawanda is Buffalo's northern inner-ring suburb, with 70,853 residents in mid-2025 and 33,965 households. Its 18.7 square miles of land run from the Niagara River in the west to Niagara Falls Boulevard, which is US 62, in the east.

The town split from Buffalo in 1836, Kenmore incorporated in 1899, and a big wave of suburban building followed in the 1940s and 1950s. Population peaked at 107,282 in 1970 and has eased since, so much of the housing stock is from that era.

Roads are an asset. Interstate 190 runs down the western side, Interstate 290 crosses to US 62, and state routes 324, 265, 266 and 384 serve the neighborhoods in between. Workers average a 20.6 minute trip. Names buyers know include Brighton, Kenilworth, Parkview, Sheridan Parkside, Green Acres and Old Town.

Ownership and price figures

A typical owner-occupied house is valued at $213,900 here, and owners live in 72.2 percent of the homes. Median household income is $77,673.

Few people move in a given year, with 90.2 percent staying put. Monthly owner costs run $1,494 with a mortgage and $662 without. Buyers will compare your house with other 1950s-era suburban homes, so condition and updates carry weight.

Schools are a selling point. Kenmore-Tonawanda Union Free School District serves most of the area and runs Kenmore West and Kenmore East high schools, while Sweet Home Central covers a smaller portion. Verify which one serves your street before you name it in an ad.

Free, no-obligation offerTell us about your Tonawanda house and get a written cash offer within 24 hours.Get My Cash Offer →

Storm water certificate of compliance

Yes, you need a certificate of compliance covering the storm water system before the sale. The Building Department arranges the inspection at (716) 877-8801, and it looks at several parts of the system.

  • The sump pump and the electric line that powers it
  • Footing drains
  • Yard drains
  • Downspouts

Book it before you list. A dead pump or a misdirected downspout takes time to fix, and the week before closing is a poor time to learn about it. Permit documents from before 1965 were destroyed, so hold on to your own receipts for older work.

A 0% Residential Rehabilitation loan secured by a mortgage on your house comes due when title transfers, so ask for a payoff figure before you set a closing date.

Tax bills and assessment appeals

The assessor's office values 28,828 parcels in the town and Kenmore, worth $10.9 billion in market value. Exemption filings and status are fixed on March 1, the tentative roll appears May 1, and the final roll is filed by July 1.

School (Ken-Ton and Sweet Home districts)October 16November 307.5%, October 15 to 31

Ask the receiver of taxes at the Town Clerk to confirm the dates and amounts on your own bill, because the schedule is reset yearly.

  • Informal review: from February 1 to April 1, email evidence of your home's value to the assessor.
  • Grievance Day: the Board of Assessment Review sits on the fourth Tuesday of May (May 25, 2027) and takes form RP-524. You may submit in writing and skip the hearing.
  • Small Claims Assessment Review: a court-run next step for an owner-occupied home of up to three families, with a $30 fee and petitions due by July 30.

Exemptions and paying a bill

Owner-occupied houses are eligible for STAR, though the state runs the program and the assessor has no power over a STAR record. If your benefit changed from a bill exemption to a credit check, let your mortgage servicer know so any escrow account is adjusted.

Other exemptions on the town's list cover seniors, disabled residents, firefighters and volunteer ambulance workers. Applications go to the assessor by March 1.

You can pay a tax bill on the town's online portal. Partial payments are different: those are taken only in person at the Town Clerk's office on weekdays, 8:30 AM to 4:00 PM.

Water, trash and the yard before closing

The town's Water Billing Department, at 716-871-8843, can stop or start service and set up a final bill, so call it once you have a closing date. Plumbing from the water meter into the house, including the meter, belongs to the homeowner. A leaky outdoor spigot or a running toilet can inflate a bill, which is worth fixing before a buyer reads your water history.

Town crews collect old paint, concrete from a homeowner's own project, bundled branches no longer than six feet and refrigerators with the doors removed. Tires go to the Highway Department at 450 Woodward Avenue in Kenmore. Clearing the garage before the inspection and showings is easier when you know what the town will take on your regular garbage day.

Keep the lawn in order too. Grass and weeds should not pass 10 inches, and a Code Enforcement Officer can fine an owner who does not cut after a 10-day notice. A vacant house with a tall lawn invites complaints, so arrange mowing if you move out before the sale closes.

Moving day checklist

Once you have a closing date, line up a few small tasks. Schedule the storm water inspection, call Water Billing about a final reading, and clear the garage and basement so the inspector can see the sump pump. Fix the yard drains and downspouts first if they are clogged.

Gather your latest tax bill and confirm the exemption you hold, because it will not carry to the buyer. Then leave the keys and meter details with your attorney or the title company.

Frequently asked questions

Is a sump pump inspection required to sell here?

Yes. The town requires a storm water certificate of compliance for a sale, and the check includes the pump, its power line and the drains and downspouts. The Building Department books it at (716) 877-8801.

Is the city of Tonawanda included here?

No. This page is for the town around Kenmore. The city is a separate municipality along the canal to the north, so ask that city's offices about its rules.

When can I contest my assessment in person?

Grievance Day is the fourth Tuesday of May, which lands on May 25 in 2027. File RP-524 with the assessor and attach comparable sales if you have them.

What happens to a town rehab loan when I sell?

The deferred loan falls due when title transfers. A sale, any change in who is on the deed, a home equity loan and moving out all trigger it, so ask the Community Development office for a payoff figure.

How quickly can an all-cash sale close here?

The date depends on the buyer and the title search, so have it put in writing. The storm water certificate and any open tax balance are the likeliest items to move it.

Selling a house in Schenectady

Most Schenectady houses were built for mill and plant workers, so a listing here turns on age, permits and tenant history more than on new finishes. The city is the seat of Schenectady County, on the Mohawk River about 15 miles northwest of Albany. Its 10.79 square miles hold 6,212.7 people per square mile, so lots are narrow and neighbors are close. You see rows of frame two-families near the old plant sites and larger homes near Union College.

Winters are cold, with January averaging near 22.9 °F, so a house that has been through many heating seasons shows it in roofs, porches and boilers. Buyers look at those first.

Housing numbers and pricing

Prices are low and renters outnumber owners. Only 45.6% of homes are lived in by their owners, a typical owner-occupied unit is valued at $168,800, and monthly rent is $1,145. A cash investor or small landlord is a natural buyer for many of these houses.

Schenectady housing profile (population as of July 1, 2025; other figures 2020-2024)
Housing measureSchenectady
Residents69,471

A citywide figure will not price your own address. A house that needs a roof or a new furnace sells for less than its block average, and one with fresh systems sells for more. Ask the assessor for your assessed value and compare it with recent sales on your street.

Neighborhoods that carry a premium

Value follows history here. The Stockade Historic District, designated in 1965 as New York's first historic district, preserves dozens of Dutch and English colonial houses. The General Electric Realty Plot beside Union College was drawn up for company executives and is counted among the nation's earliest planned residential neighborhoods.

The riverfront looks different from a decade ago. Rivers Casino and Resort opened in February 2017 on a former locomotive works site, and the same development brought a marina, hotels, apartments and condominiums.

If you are selling inside a historic district, speak to the building department before repainting for showings. Painting is among the few jobs the city exempts from permits, and the exemption stops at historic district lines.

Free, no-obligation offerTell us about your Schenectady house and get a written cash offer within 24 hours.Get My Cash Offer →

Permits for repairs before you list

Nearly every repair, alteration or addition needs a building permit from the City of Schenectady Building Department, and painting is the notable exception. Permits run for 12 months. When you hire a contractor, the department's rule is that the contractor files for the permit, not you. It accepts applications online, by mail to Room 17 at 105 Jay Street, or by fax, and asks you to allow at least 24 hours for processing.

Skipping a permit risks a stop work order and fines, and it can stall a closing if the buyer's lender wants a certificate of completion or occupancy. A Certificate of Ordinary Repair lists small jobs a homeowner can do without a permit. Questions about a specific repair go to 518-382-5050.

  • Expect to supply a scope of work, materials, dimensions and a cost estimate.
  • Electrical and plumbing jobs call for contractors with the required trade credentials where they apply.
  • Workers compensation coverage, or a personal waiver for self-performed work, is part of the packet.
  • Pools need both a building permit and an electrical permit, obtained by the installer.

Selling a house with tenants or a rental history

The city treats any house rented to tenants as a registered rental, and each tenancy needs its own certificate. Landlord registration is step one. The form calls for verified owner information, a named agent if the owner lives outside Schenectady County, a current insurance declaration or bond, and a notary's signature.

Step two is the rental inspection, at $50 per unit. Multi-unit buildings are inspected unit by unit, while single-family rental homes and owner-occupied two-families are exempt from the inspection. Passing earns a rental certificate valid for the present tenancy, or up to three years in a building with three or more units. A new certificate is required whenever one tenant leaves and another arrives, and if no tenant is recorded within 30 days of an inspection, the unit must be inspected again.

Buyers of two- and three-family houses tend to ask for this paper trail, so pull your registration and certificates before you list. Renting without a current certificate violates the city code and can bring fines, fees and possibly jail. A cash buyer will still ask what the file looks like, but can usually take the property as is.

Tax bills, installments and assessment appeals

The city bills once a year, on January 1, and accepts payment in four installments due in January, April, July and October. That single bill rolls together city and county tax, water and sewer charges, and the trash fee where one applies. School tax is billed separately by the school district.

The City Assessment Office in Room 8 at City Hall handles disputes; its number is 518-382-5075. Each year the grievance window opens on May 1, when the tentative roll comes out, and closes late in May. Applications can be mailed, emailed or handed in, and an owner who skips the board hearing is not penalized for it.

Closing figures split the installments between buyer and seller by date. Call the Bureau of Receipts in Room 100 ahead of time and ask for the paid-through status of each quarter.

Sell as-isNo repairs, no cleaning and no showings. We buy Schenectady houses in any condition.See My Cash Offer →

Transfer tax and filing the deed

New York charges two dollars per five hundred of price on a conveyance, and the seller normally bears it. Buyers pay an extra 1% only on residences at $1 million or above. The return, Form TP-584, goes to the Schenectady County Clerk, and the form and money are due by the fifteenth day after the deed is delivered.

One wrinkle for investors: when an LLC buys or sells a building of up to four units, the state will not take the return without documents naming the LLC's members, managers and other authorized people.

A quick checklist before you list

Walk through the house and make a short list of anything a buyer or inspector will notice: roof, porch, boiler, wiring. Then call the Building Department at 518-382-5050 to learn what permits are open at your address. Gather the rental registration and certificates if tenants have lived there, and ask the Bureau of Receipts for the paid-through status of your tax installments.

With that folder ready, you can decide between a listing and a direct cash offer. A listing suits a house in good shape on a block with strong recent sales. A cash offer suits a house that needs work, has tenants you would rather not manage through showings, or has an open permit you do not want to finish.

Frequently asked questions

Will open code violations stop a Schenectady sale?

They will not stop one by law, but they travel with the house. Ask the Building Department what is open at your address and hand buyers a written list before they sign.

Who covers the state transfer tax?

The seller pays it unless the contract says otherwise, at two dollars per five hundred of price. If the seller does not pay, the state looks to the buyer, who can then recover it from the seller.

Do I need a rental certificate to close on a rented house?

Closing does not require one, yet renting without a current certificate breaks city code. Lenders and buyers of multi-unit houses often want to see the registration and certificates.

When can I appeal my assessment?

Each May. The window opens May 1 and closes late in the month. Call the assessment office at 518-382-5075 for the exact date.

Where does the TP-584 transfer form go?

To the Schenectady County Clerk, with payment, by the fifteenth day after the deed is delivered. Most closing attorneys and title agents file it together with the deed.

How quickly can a Utica house change hands?

Speed in Utica comes down to the route. Owners tend to pick between an agent's listing, a sale they run on their own, and an outright purchase by someone willing to take the building with its flaws.

Open-market buyers need showings, an inspection and a bank's appraisal, and that sequence takes weeks. A direct purchase fits a vacant property, an inherited one, a rental with a hard tenant, or a building the city has already cited. On any route, three offices handle the paperwork for a city address: the City Assessor, the Oneida County Clerk and the Codes Department.

Utica housing numbers

Renters and owners split the city almost evenly. With the middle home value at $151,300, one new roof or boiler can eat a large part of the sale price, and that is why repair costs drive many decisions here.

About half of Utica's households rent, so if tenants live in your building, build the sale timeline around their leases.

Where Utica sits and what shaped its houses

Utica is where Oneida County's offices sit, set on the Mohawk River in central New York, roughly midway between Albany and Syracuse. The city spans roughly 17 square miles, 456 feet above sea level, in a wide river floodplain with gently sloping ground.

It received a village charter in 1798 and a city charter in 1832. The Erie Canal arrived in 1825 and the Chenango Canal and the railroads followed, which fed furniture, textile, lumber and firearms makers. Much of the older housing dates from that era, and many streets run parallel to the river instead of on a strict grid.

  • West Utica, historically a German, Irish and Polish area, and East Utica, long associated with Italian families.
  • Corn Hill near the city center and the Triangle neighborhood north of downtown.
  • Genesee Street and Oriskany Street frame the historic downtown around Bagg's Square.

The Utica City School District boundary matches the city line.

Winter and a Utica house

Winter puts the most strain on a Utica house. The city sits in a valley open to north winds and gets lake-effect snow, with average annual snowfall near 102 inches and January lows around 13 degrees Fahrenheit.

Buyers and their inspectors look closely at anything the cold punishes. Before listing or accepting an offer, walk through the house with that in mind.

  • Roof edges, gutters and attic insulation, where ice dams form.
  • Pipes along exterior walls and in unheated basements.
  • Furnace or boiler age and the last service date.
  • Driveway and steps that stay safe to walk when snow-covered.

An empty house in January still needs enough heat to protect the plumbing, and your insurer should know if it will sit vacant during the sale.

Codes Department and violations

The Codes Department enforces the New York State Building and Property Maintenance Code, reviews building plans and inspects construction. It also inspects dwellings of people who receive Oneida County social services programs, under a contract with the county.

A cited owner receives a Notice and Order with a deadline. If the work is not done, this is what follows:

  • An extension may be granted if you request it in writing before the deadline.
  • An appearance ticket can send the case to Utica City Court, where the penalty under city code section 2-12-5 can reach $500, up to 15 days in jail, or both.
  • The case can move to Supreme Court, which can order repairs or demolition, and the city can add its costs to the property's taxes.
  • A dangerous building can be closed, and it needs a new Certificate of Occupancy with electrical, plumbing, fire safety and codes inspections before it reopens.

Open violations and unpaid city costs stay with the property. Ask Codes what is on file for your address before deciding on a number.

Property tax due dates

Utica owners receive three bills a year. City tax is paid in installments due at the end of April and the end of July, school tax is due on the first Tuesday of October and the first Tuesday of December, and the third city installment together with the Oneida County bill falls at the end of January.

Late penalties on city tax are 2 percent in the first five days and 5 percent from day six, then 1 percent more each month. The city can foreclose two years after the original bill date, and delinquent taxes can be paid off in installments.

Request exact payoff figures from the Comptroller, since city, school and county bills are issued on different dates.

Assessment calendar

The City Assessor's office works on four fixed dates, and an owner who misses the exemption deadline waits another year for the savings.

  • March 1: last day to file any exemption application with the assessor.
  • May 1: tentative assessment roll is filed.
  • July 1: final roll is filed, including changes from the Board of Assessment Review.
  • July 1 of the prior year: taxable status and valuation date, which fixes the ownership and condition that are assessed.

Buyers of a Utica house should also file an address change with the Assessor's office, because tax bills follow the mailing address on record.

Recording a deed for a Utica house

Utica adds a step ahead of the county. Property inside the city line needs the City Assessor's stamp on the deed before the Oneida County Clerk will take it. The assessor asks for the original signed deed, never a copy, plus a finished RP-5217 form, and charges $30 in cash or a check payable to the City of Utica.

After the stamp, the deed goes to the county. Oneida's clerk charges a $45 statutory fee, $5 per written side of each page, $5 to file the TP-584, and $125 for the RP-5217 on a residence. The seller owes $2 on every $500 of price, and the transfer return follows the deed within 15 days of delivery.

The county also demands a legal description, both parties' full names and street addresses, and original notarized signatures. Corrections by white-out or redaction cause a rejection, which can hold up a closing, so let your attorney or title agent review the deed before submitting it.

What to have ready

Gather your deed, the latest bills from the city, school and county, and any notice from the Codes Department. Ask the Comptroller for payoff figures and the City Assessor about the deed stamp, then book your attorney or title agent early so the stamp, the RP-5217 and the TP-584 are ready on the same day.

If tenants live in the house, add their leases to the folder. An outright cash purchase can take an occupied or cited building as it stands, but the buyer will still want the facts before naming a price.

Is a two-week cash closing realistic in Utica?

It can be, when title is clean and every owner signs. Estate paperwork, tenants or an open code case slow things down, so settle those items first.

Who stamps a deed in Utica?

The City Assessor does, before the Oneida County Clerk records it. The office wants the original signed deed and the RP-5217 form, and the stamp costs $30.

What does a typical Utica home cost?

The middle value for 2020 to 2024 is $151,300, with rent near $951 a month. Condition and the number of units move any one building well above or below that.

Can a house with open violations still sell?

Yes. The notices stay with the building, so any buyer will price them in. Get the open notices and their deadlines from the Codes Department first.

What is the next school tax date?

The second school installment falls on the first Tuesday of December. The combined city and county installment comes due at the end of January.

Speed depends mostly on the file. An open permit, a missing certificate or an unpaid installment tends to stall a closing once the attorneys start reviewing, whatever the buyer's financing. The sections below cover the documents, the tax calendar and the recording steps that set the pace.

Neighborhoods buyers search by

White Plains has been Westchester's county seat since 1758 and became a city in 1916. A late 1960s urban renewal plan reshaped the downtown core around the county courthouse, the Galleria mall and office towers, and City Center later added two 35-story residential towers. Offices, hospitals and courts keep the weekday population far above the resident count.

Dozens of named neighborhoods exist, and buyers search by them. A few of the better known:

Trains, roads and schools

Commuting access is the feature buyers mention first. Metro-North's Harlem Line stops twice in the city, downtown at Main Street and the Bronx River and again in North White Plains, and an express run to Midtown takes about 31 minutes.

  • Rail: both city stations are on the Harlem Line.

  • Air: Westchester County Airport sits in Harrison, about seven miles northeast.

Since 1988 the city's public schools have run a parents' choice program for elementary placement. Families may rank schools on factors other than distance, so an address does not lock in one elementary school.

Certificate of Occupancy and the Building Department

Under the city's rule, no building may be occupied, and no occupancy class changed, before the Commissioner of Building issues a Certificate of Occupancy. The department works from 70 Church Street, phone 914-422-1269.

Every permitted job must be completed and inspected by the Building Department, the Fire Department and any other agency involved. For a missing certificate, owners file a Building Short Form with the Updated and Substitute CO type, plus the fee, after which a code enforcement officer inspects.   • A Certificate of Compliance covers decks, additions and alterations that leave the building's use unchanged.

A missing certificate is best resolved before listing, because a buyer's attorney is likely to ask for it.

Tax due dates and water bills at closing

Three payments fall due each year, and the last day of the due month is the cutoff. After that, interest runs at 1 percent per month, and the Finance Department cannot waive it.

  • January 1: second half of the city and school levy, late from February 1.
  • April 1: the county levy, late from May 1.

Bills go out in mid-December, late March and June. Under Real Property Tax Law Section 922 a bill that fails to arrive changes nothing, so call the Finance Department at 914-422-1248 if yours is missing. Make checks payable to the Commissioner of Finance, 255 Main Street, Room 102.

Water adds a seller's task. A final reading costs $75 and is requested at 914-422-1211, and unpaid water charges come back onto the property as a tax lien on the following July 1. Ownership on the tax roll changes only after the Assessor's Office gets a certified copy of the recorded deed. Challenging a White Plains assessment

The Assessor's Office runs on a fixed yearly calendar, and the complaint window is short. December 1 is the taxable status date, the tentative roll is dated January 1, complaints are taken January 1 to 21, and the final roll lands on March 1. Exemptions are handled from April 1 through December 1.

One assessed value drives both the city and school bills, so a seller who finds it too high should collect recent nearby sales before January. The office is at 255 Main Street, phone 914-422-1223.

Recording a White Plains deed

The state charges the seller a base transfer tax per $500 of price, rounded up to the next $500, and the buyer owes an added 1 percent when a residence sells for $1 million or more. Form TP-584 travels with the deed to the county clerk, and payment is due within 15 days of delivery.

The Westchester County Clerk's Land Records Division takes a deed only with four documents generated in its PREP system: a recording cover sheet, the TP-584, the RP-5217 transfer report and a payment cover sheet. Originals come back after scanning, and anyone needing a certified copy fast should order it with the submission.

The owner of record, until the Assessor's Office is sent a certified copy of the recorded deed. Send it promptly, and file the city's Tax Account Change Form if the bill needs a new mailing address.

The seller pays, unless the contract assigns it to the buyer. The tax is $2 for each $500 of price, rounded up to the next $500.

What if no White Plains tax bill arrives?

The tax and any interest are still owed. Call the Finance Department at 914-422-1248 to verify the address and request a duplicate.

From January 1 to January 21 each year. The next one opens January 1, 2027, against the tentative roll.

Choosing how to sell in Hamburg

Three paths are open to a Hamburg seller: an agent, a do-it-yourself sale, or a buyer who pays cash and takes the house as it is. Cash is quickest. A Southtowns listing might bring a higher price, but expect open houses, an appraisal and the repair list a buyer's inspector writes. Erie County stacks its own transfer tax on the state tax, which shrinks the check you receive.

  • Listing: makes sense for a house that shows well, if waiting for a mortgage buyer is fine.
  • Do it yourself: the commission is yours, along with the contract and state forms.
  • As-is cash sale: for inherited houses, put-off maintenance, empty properties and tenant problems.

Hamburg at a glance

Hamburg is a 41-square-mile town on the Lake Erie shore south of Buffalo. Two villages, Hamburg and Blasdell, sit inside it, together with Wanakah and lakefront hamlets like Athol Springs and Lake View. The 2025 population was 60,768, up 1.2% from 60,064 in 2020, in 26,440 households of about 2.24 people. Owners live in 75.4% of homes, and the median value is $251,100. The median renter pays $1,106, the middle household earns $88,651, and the commute averages 23.0 minutes. Moving is uncommon, with 91.7% of residents in the same home a year earlier.

Repairs eat a big share of the price at these values. Get quotes first, then decide between fixing up and selling as is. The Thruway (I-90), US 62, US 20 and NY 5 cross the town, and five NFTA bus lines serve it.

  • Village of Hamburg: the center along Main Street, close to the fairgrounds.
  • Blasdell: the second village.
  • Lakeshore hamlets: Athol Springs, Wanakah and Lake View, served mainly by the Frontier district.

Frontier Central serves the lakeshore and most of the area outside the village, while Hamburg Central serves the village and adjoining streets. West Seneca and Orchard Park districts reach small portions along the town line. Buyers see whichever school tax line your parcel carries, so read the bill before you advertise.

Preparing for a lake-effect winter question

Winter comes up at nearly every Hamburg showing, and a quick answer helps. Snow totaled 81.2 inches from November 16 to 18, 2022, and visitors will study the roof, gutters and furnace. Take photos of each, save the service receipts, and have them ready to hand to a buyer or an inspector.

Assessment and tax dates

The town assessor lists 26,032 parcels and an equalization rate of 29%. Values were last reset in 1990, which makes recent sale prices a better guide for a buyer than the assessment.

Hamburg assessment and tax dates
Assessment or tax stepDate
Taxable status dateMarch 1
Tentative roll / final rollMay 1 / July 1

Town and county tax, no penalty throughFebruary 15

The assessor meets owners informally from July 2 to April 25 and asks you to bring any recent appraisal. The office also checks MLS data against its records and may send a notice for an inspection when a sale shows a change. A USPS postmark dated on the deadline avoids a penalty, with no exceptions. After town collection closes, bills still unpaid are handed to Erie County Real Property in Buffalo.

What Erie County charges to record a Hamburg deed

The Erie County Clerk handles Hamburg deeds. Recording begins with a $45 statutory fee, plus $5 for every written side of a page. The TP-584 transfer tax form is $10, and a residential Real Property Transfer Report is $125.

In Erie County the seller owes $4.50 for each $500 of price, made up of $2.00 for the state and $2.50 for the county. Round the price up to the next $500. The money is due at the counter when the deed is presented.

  • Senior reduction: if you are 62 or older and have lived in your one- or two-family home for a year or more, the rate is $2.00 per $500, not $4.50.
  • New construction: the county portion may not apply when a residence was built on previously unimproved land, so ask the clerk.
  • Mansion tax: a 1% charge at $1 million or more, which the buyer pays.

The clerk hands out the senior affidavit at no cost. Count the county's share when you estimate proceeds.

Selling with school or town tax still due

You can settle an open bill at the closing table, but find out the amount beforehand. Town and county tax is penalty-free through February 15 and school tax through October 15. Once the town's collection season ends, an unpaid bill moves to Erie County Real Property in Buffalo, which means a different office and a different payoff. Your attorney or the title company can confirm the current balance and which office holds it.

If payments have fallen behind and that is why you're selling, a direct buyer can pay the balance out of the purchase price and leave you the rest. Weigh that against a listing that might pay more but takes months and repair spending.

What happens after you accept an offer

After you choose a buyer, contracts are exchanged and a title search follows. That search turns up open school or town tax, liens and permit trouble, and each item is paid or credited at the closing. You then sign the deed and transfer forms, your lender is paid off from the proceeds, and the deed travels to the Erie County Clerk along with the tax and fees. Because transfer tax is due on presentation, it is settled as part of the closing.

Documents to have ready

  • A recent appraisal, if you have one, for an informal talk with the assessor.
  • School and town tax bills, plus any notice from Erie County Real Property.
  • Service records for the roof, gutters and furnace.
  • Mortgage payoff figure and any liens.
  • For owners 62 or older, the senior transfer tax affidavit from the clerk's office.

A cash sale in Hamburg

Buying with cash means accepting the flaws, so nobody haggles over repairs and no lender holds up the schedule. Title work, tax proration and recording continue as usual. Put each buyer's price, date and transfer tax arrangement in writing. Then set your net after the county share beside a listing's net after commission and repairs.

Frequently asked questions

Who handles the transfer tax when a Hamburg house sells?

The seller pays both the state and the Erie County portions, a combined $4.50 per $500 of price. It is due when the deed is handed in for recording, so it comes out of your proceeds at closing.

Does a senior discount exist for Hamburg sellers?

Yes. Erie County lowers the rate to $2.00 per $500 for sellers aged 62 or older who have owned and lived in a one- or two-family home for at least a year. The affidavit is free at the clerk's office.

When is the last day to pay Hamburg school tax without penalty?

The school deadline is October 15, and the town and county deadline is February 15. A mailed payment counts if the envelope carries a USPS postmark of that date, and the town makes no exceptions.

What should I show a buyer who asks about Hamburg winters?

Show roof age, furnace and gutter service records. Lake Erie dropped a recorded 81.2 inches of snow in three days in November 2022, and buyers here expect proof the house handles it.

Can I contest my Hamburg assessment?

You can file form RP-524 for the annual review hearing held late each May. The assessor will also meet you informally from July 2 through April 25 if you bring a recent appraisal.

Sell My House Fast in Clay, NY: Options, Costs and Cash Offers

Last updated November 14, 2026.

Selling in Clay?
We buy Clay houses as-is, with no commission, no repairs and no closing costs to you.

Which way to sell a Clay house

Three routes are open to a Clay owner: an agent listing, a sale without an agent, or an as-is purchase by a cash buyer. Which one wins depends on the calendar, the condition of the roof and mechanicals, and whether you can keep paying the mortgage and the January tax bill while a house sits on the market.

A listing exposes the house to the most buyers, yet it means cleaning, staging, weekend showings and a buyer whose lender may balk at an appraisal. A cash purchase trims that list to a walkthrough and a closing date. Expect a cash number to land under a polished listing price, so line the two up on what you would actually keep after payoff, taxes and fees.

  • An agent suits a tidy house and an owner with months to spare.
  • A sale without an agent suits someone who already knows the buyer, such as a neighbor or relative.
  • A cash buyer suits a rental with tenants, an inherited house, a property that needs work or a move with a hard deadline.

Clay housing and neighborhoods

Clay is the largest town in Onondaga County, set just north of Syracuse. The Oneida River forms the northern boundary with Oswego County, and the Seneca River runs along the western edge. Retail clusters along NY Route 31, and NY Route 481 meets it near Euclid.

Buyers see two kinds of housing. Planned subdivisions such as Fairway East, Lawton Valley Hunt, Country Meadow and The Farmstead sit next to older hamlets including Euclid, Moyers Corners, Belgium and Three Rivers. Most of the housing dates from a postwar surge, when the population rose from 7,001 in 1950 to 36,274 in 1970 and 52,838 by 1980. Houses built in that stretch are now fifty to seventy years old, which is why roofs, windows and heating systems come up in so many Clay sales. The town had 60,527 people in 2020 and an estimated 59,285 in July 2025.

Clay housing and income, 2020 to 2024
MeasureClay
Share of homes lived in by owners71.2%
Middle value of an owner-lived-in home$205,900
Median gross rent$1,240

Median household income$90,707

A median sits in the middle of the range, so a house with worn systems may price well below $205,900. Mailing addresses vary by corner of town: ZIP codes include 13041 for Clay, 13090 for Bayberry, 13212 for North Syracuse, 13088 for Liverpool and 13029 for Brewerton.

School districts and tax rates

Five school districts reach into the town. Liverpool and North Syracuse are the two largest, with smaller pieces belonging to Baldwinsville, Phoenix and Central Square. The district printed on a bill often steers how buyers think about a house.

It also steers the cost. The assessor's tax page shows school rates per thousand dollars of full market value running from $18.58 in Central Square to $28.21 in Liverpool, with North Syracuse at $23.22. The county rate is $5.14. Town levies add $1.94 for highways, $0.96 for fire protection and $0.75 for administration, and a county sewer charge of $417.07 applies to each residential unit. Call the assessor for the rates in force for the current year before you quote any of these.

Five volunteer fire departments protect the town under contract, and the Town runs one water district. Buyers read every line, so have a recent bill ready.

Free, no-obligation offerTell us about your Clay house and get a written cash offer within 24 hours.Get My Cash Offer →

Tax calendar and payment

Most parcels get two bills a year: Town and County in January and school in the fall. Houses in the Village of North Syracuse get a third, a village bill in early summer. The Tax Receiver collects all of them.

  • Town and County: mailed around January 1, due without penalty January 31.
  • School: mailed around September 1, due without penalty around October 1.
  • North Syracuse village: mailed around June 1, due without penalty July 1.
  • Water: the Tax Office also takes payments for the Town's single water district.

Because parcels sit in different districts, the September bill can differ sharply between two similar houses on neighboring streets. If your house is inside the Village of North Syracuse, the summer village bill is an extra one that owners outside the village never see.

You can pay through the Onondaga County Department of Finance website, mail a check, or use the secured drop box outside Town Hall at 4401 State Route 31. The title company will split these bills between you and the buyer on the closing statement. Get a current payoff figure from the Tax Receiver before closing instead of leaning on last year's paper.

Assessments and Grievance Day

State law sets the assessor's year. March 1 is the taxable status date and also the last day to file any exemption, with no exceptions. May 1 brings the tentative roll, the fourth Tuesday in May is Grievance Day, and July 1 makes the roll final. The hearing runs from 4 to 8 p.m. at Town Hall. A grievance form and filing instructions are posted on the Town site.

Values on the roll drive both the September school bill and the January Town and County bill, and they stay put until the next taxable status year. A grievance will not rescue a sale already in motion, but the roll still tells a buyer's lender the taxable value.

The assessor handles senior, disability and limited-income, agricultural, clergy, nonprofit and commercial or industrial exemptions, along with military service exemptions. Basic STAR is registered through New York State rather than the Town.

Permits, deeds and utilities

The Town's department directory lists the assessor, code enforcement, planning and development, highway, the Tax Receiver, the Town Clerk and water. Code enforcement covers building permits, inspections and zoning compliance, so it is the office to ask about a finished basement or a deck that went up without paperwork.

The Onondaga County Clerk, not the Town, files deeds. New York charges transfer tax of $2 per $500 of consideration, normally on the seller, and Form TP-584 goes to the clerk with the deed no later than 15 days after delivery. Call the clerk for current recording charges. The Town Clerk keeps local records.

A cash sale does not change who records the deed or who bills the taxes. It changes the pace: with no lender appraisal or underwriting, the title search and the payoff letters are the main items still to arrange.

Before closing, make sure open permits are closed and that no unpaid water or sewer balance sits on the parcel. Collect the deed, the latest tax bills and any mortgage payoff statement, and the closing attorney can move quickly.

Frequently asked questions

Does a Clay house with deferred repairs still sell?

Yes, though the price follows the work. A buyer who takes the house as is expects a discount for the roof, furnace or siding. Ask code enforcement about open permits first, because those can delay any closing.

Who bills property tax on a Clay house?

The Clay Tax Receiver bills Town, County, school and North Syracuse village taxes for parcels inside the Town. Town and County payments are due January 31 and school payments around October 1.

When is Grievance Day in Clay?

The fourth Tuesday of May, with hearings from 4 to 8 p.m. at Town Hall. File any exemption application by March 1.

Which school district serves my Clay address?

It varies by parcel across Liverpool, North Syracuse, Baldwinsville, Phoenix and Central Square. The school bill names the district, and the Tax Receiver can confirm it.

Where does a Clay deed get recorded?

At the Onondaga County Clerk. Call that office for current forms and fees before you set a closing date.

Selling in Union?

Ways to sell a house in Union

Owners in Broome County's Union have an agent, a do-it-yourself sale or an all-cash buyer to choose from. This page covers the whole town: the villages of Endicott and Johnson City, plus hamlets such as Endwell, Union Center, West Corners and Westover.

A listing can fetch the top price for a house in good shape, at the cost of showings, inspections and waiting on a buyer's mortgage. Selling for cash gives up some of that upside in return for a simpler path, which helps if you face repairs, a tenant, an inherited property or a move with a deadline.

  • Agent: the most exposure and preparation, and financing contingencies from buyers.
  • By owner: you save the commission and do all the paperwork yourself.
  • All cash: the house is bought as is and the two sides agree on a closing date.

Whatever you choose, sort out the town's paperwork first. The code office letter described below is the item to request first.

Union and its housing market

Union sits on the north side of the Susquehanna River, west of Binghamton, and is one of the Triple Cities along with Johnson City and Endicott. It has 53,972 residents as of July 1, 2025, a 3.9 percent drop from the 2020 base of 56,161, across 35.44 square miles of land. Population peaked at 64,490 in 1970.

Getting around is straightforward: NY 17 crosses the river here, NY 26 and NY 38B meet near Union Center, NY 17C runs across the south, and Tri-Cities Airport sits in the southwest corner.

Owner-occupied homes have a median value of $149,900, owners live in 58.9 percent of homes, and there are 24,963 households. Rent runs $936 at the median and household income is $61,713. Mean travel time to work is 17.7 minutes, a short commute that buyers working in Binghamton will notice.

Assessments and the tax calendar

The town assessor keeps tax maps for roughly 23,000 parcels. The town is not at 100 percent assessment, so New York State issues an equalization rate each year that reflects the average ratio of assessed value to market value, based mainly on arm's-length sales from the previous year.

That matters when you read your bill: an assessed value is not the town's opinion of what your house would sell for. Ask the assessor for the current equalization rate before you compare your assessment to an offer.

Town of Union assessment calendar
DateWhat it means
March 1Taxable status date; what is on the property that day is reflected in the July 1 roll
May 1Tentative roll presented, no changes afterward
Fourth Tuesday in MayGrievance Board meets to hear complaints
July 1Final roll takes effect and cannot change until the next July 1 except by court order

The Grievance Board has three members, acts independently of the assessor and meets once a year. In 2027 the fourth Tuesday in May falls on May 25. The tentative roll is viewable online within the first 10 days of May.

Free, no-obligation offerTell us about your Union house and get a written cash offer within 24 hours.Get My Cash Offer →

Exemption filing windows

The Assessor's Office accepts military service exemptions and new Enhanced STAR applications, for people turning 65 who now hold Basic STAR, between September 1 and March 1. Exemptions that depend on current income, such as the low-income senior and disability exemptions, are accepted only from January 15 to March 1.

  • New homeowners apply for STAR directly through the New York State Tax Department.
  • Enhanced STAR applicants need the prior year's income statement or tax return.
  • The town also offers a home improvement exemption, with a form on its forms page.

Because these windows fall in winter, an owner who sells in the spring should check that the exemption was filed for the current roll, and a buyer should ask the assessor which exemptions on the current bill will end at closing.

Code office letter and certificates of occupancy

New buildings and additions need a certificate of occupancy before use, and most lenders now require one before issuing a mortgage. For an existing building, the Code Enforcement staff issues a letter stating that the building is a legal nonconforming use, and those letters are also necessary when properties are sold.

Request it early, and ask the code staff what they need to see for your address. Building permit fees, inspection rules and junk vehicle and weed rules are all posted on the town site if you need to fix an exterior problem before buyers visit.

Flood history

The town's flood management office keeps recovery documents from the 2011 flooding that followed Tropical Storm Lee, including FEMA buyout program materials. If your lot is mapped in a flood zone, an insurer will ask about it, so gather elevation and insurance records before listing. A cash buyer will often take a house with a flood past as it is, while a mortgage buyer's insurer may slow the file.

Sell as-isNo repairs, no cleaning and no showings. We buy Union houses in any condition.See My Cash Offer →

Recording a sale with the Broome County Clerk

The Broome County Clerk records deeds at the Broome County Office Building, 60 Hawley Street in Binghamton. Posted charges are $45 plus $5 per page for the deed, $10 for the TP-584 transfer tax return and $125 for the RP-5217 on a residential property.

Transfer tax in Broome County is $5 per $1,000 of price, with $4 going to the State and $1 to Broome County, and the full $5 is paid with the return. The sale price is rounded up to the next $500 to compute it.

  • The seller signs the deed before a notary, and the names must match on the deed, TP-584 and RP-5217.
  • Both the seller and the buyer sign the TP-584 and the RP-5217.
  • Out-of-state sellers also file form IT-2663, the nonresident estimated income tax payment.
  • A recorded deed cannot be amended. Fixing an error or changing who owns the house takes a new deed, so read the draft closely before you sign.
  • Send documents as originals, not photocopies, and include a self-addressed stamped envelope for their return.
  • Deeds back to 1963 can be searched on the clerk's website, and copies are $0.65 per page at the office.

The clerk also offers a free Fraud Alert that emails you whenever a deed or mortgage is recorded under your name.

Before you sign a contract

Pull together the tax bill, any code office letter, flood or insurance records and the deed, then ask the assessor what exemptions on your bill will end at closing. A buyer who sees a clean file will make a firmer offer.

A cash buyer can close on a date you pick and take the house with its flaws, which helps when repairs, a tenant or an inherited title slow a regular sale. Whoever you choose, ask for the terms in writing and have your attorney check the deed, the TP-584 and the RP-5217 for matching names before anyone signs.

Frequently asked questions

Are Endicott and Johnson City part of Union?

Yes, as villages inside the town, alongside hamlets such as Endwell, Union Center and West Corners. Confirm with the assessor which taxing jurisdictions apply to your address.

When does the Grievance Board meet?

On the fourth Tuesday of May, which is May 25 in 2027. A three-member board hears complaints about the tentative roll filed May 1.

What are the county's deed recording charges?

$45 plus $5 a page for the deed, $10 for the TP-584 and $125 for the RP-5217 on a residential parcel, before transfer tax.

Do I need a letter from the town code office to sell?

A letter from Code Enforcement stating legal nonconforming use is necessary when properties are sold. Ask the code staff what applies to your address, especially after any conversion or unpermitted work.

Can I sell a Union house with flood history?

Yes, though you should collect records first. The town keeps documents from the 2011 recovery, including FEMA buyout program materials, and insurers and buyers may raise the subject.

Selling in Troy?
