The Receiver's office assists title companies, lenders and realtors, so a payoff request from your closing team is routine. The assessor's page also carries exemption renewal notices and the volunteer firefighter exemption.

Public Works before you list

Building inspection, code enforcement, planning and zoning, and water and sewer all sit under the Department of Public Works at 1100 Sunrise Boulevard. A buyer's attorney will usually ask whether work on the house was permitted, so a quick call to that office before you list can save a delay later.

  • Ask whether any open permits or code complaints are attached to your address.
  • Look at the Official Zoning Map if you own a two-family or a commercial-looking parcel.
  • If you rent the property out, ask whether the Multi-dwelling Fire and Property Maintenance Permit Application applies.
  • Confirm your water meter and sewer status on the same call.

The department also posts a building department handout and a fee schedule. Closing a small paperwork gap now is usually cheaper than renegotiating a price over it in week three of a contract.

The state levies $2 on every $500 of price, rounded up, and the seller carries it by default. A separate 1% buyer tax begins at $1 million. Your attorney prepares the paperwork, so settle in advance who pays each recording item.

School districts for the listing

Rotterdam is served by Mohonasen Central School District and Schalmont Central School District. Streets in Colonial Manor are split between the two, so put the district on your fact sheet. The average trip to work is 22.5 minutes, and the Thruway crossing town is a selling point for anyone working in Schenectady or beyond.

What slows a closing, and how to prevent it

Most delays come from three places: title, taxes and permits. An unclear deed, an unpaid tax balance or an unpermitted addition can hold up the date, while the recording step at the county clerk is routine. Call the Receiver for the balance and ask for it in writing, call Public Works about open permits, and give your attorney the deed early. A cash buyer works without a lender's inspection, so worn systems do not block a deal, though the price will reflect the repairs. Will a buyer take my Rotterdam house with deferred maintenance?

How do I learn what taxes are owed on a Rotterdam parcel?

In May. The assessor's calendar sets grievance day on the fourth Tuesday of that month, after the May 1 tentative roll. Complaints go to the assessor, not the Receiver.

Cicero at a glance

Cicero is a lakeside suburb of Syracuse in the northeastern part of Onondaga County. Oneida Lake lies along its northern edge, the Oneida River marks the border with Oswego County, and Chittenango Creek marks the line with Madison County. The town covers about 48.5 square miles, and Cicero Swamp takes up a large part of the southeast. Interstate 81, U.S. Route 11 and Routes 31 and 298 pass through.

The 2020 census counted 31,435 residents, 0.8 percent fewer than the 31,682 of 2010.

Neighborhoods and school districts

Much of the town is wetland, forest and farm land, with new housing developments spreading onto the farmland. Hamlets include Brewerton near the northern line, Bridgeport (partly in Madison County), Cicero Center on Route 31, and shoreline settlements such as Kraus Landing, Forest Beach and Lower South Bay. The Village of North Syracuse lies partly inside the town on its western edge.

Four school districts bill taxes on Cicero parcels. The town's tax receiver processes school taxes for North Syracuse Central Schools, and for the Chittenango, Central Square and East Syracuse-Minoa districts on properties in the town. Buyers will ask which district serves an address, and the school line on the tax bill answers it.

  • Subdivisions include Bay Colony near South Bay, The Crossings, and Lyon's Runne near Oneida Lake.
  • Lakeshore settlements such as Kraus Landing and Valentine's Beach sit on Oneida Lake north of Cicero Center.

Assessment and Grievance Day

The Assessor's office values every parcel in Cicero, handles senior, disability and military exemptions, and tracks sales data and the equalization rate. The town reports a 53 percent level of assessment, so assessed values run well below market value. Judge an assessment against that ratio, not against the price you expect to get.

The next Board of Assessment Review date posted by the town is Tuesday, May 25, 2027, with hearings by appointment only at the Cicero Town Meeting Room, 8236 Brewerton Road, from 12 to 2 p.m. and 6 to 8 p.m. Complaints must be filed by 3:00 p.m. that day on form RP-524, and the town takes them in the Town Hall drop box, by mail or by email.

  • Taxable status date is March 1, and completed exemption applications may be submitted through March 1, 2027.
  • From 2026 the State decides who qualifies for the Basic and Enhanced STAR exemptions, so STAR questions go to the State, not the Assessor.
  • Informal reviews with the Assessor happen before Grievance Day, and the final roll is dated July 1.

Property tax due dates

Cicero's Receiver of Taxes processes the town and county bill, the North Syracuse village bill and the school bills. The town and county bill is mailed around January 1 and is due without penalty on February 2. School bills are mailed around September 1 and are due without penalty around October 1. Village bills for the part of North Syracuse in town are mailed around June 1 and due July 1.

Partial payments are accepted if nothing delinquent is owed, and the first payment must reach the office by the no-penalty date. Town and county bills can be split into up to four payments, village bills into three, and school bills into three. Mail counts as paid on its postmark date, but a postage meter mark does not count.

Sellers should call the tax office right after a sale. It takes two to three months after a deed is filed with the county for the Assessor's records to show the new owner, and until then the bill goes to the owner on file. Hand the new owner any bill that arrives after closing.

Zoning, permits and certificates of occupancy

The Department of Zoning and Planning issues building permits and enforces the town code from the Town Hall on Brewerton Road. A Certificate of Occupancy is issued once all work under a permit is complete and outside inspection certificates for plumbing and electrical have been received. Anything built without a permit cannot receive a Certificate of Occupancy or a Certificate of Compliance, and the town may issue a stop work order and fines.

Find your zoning on the tax bill or the town zoning map. These are the permit triggers the office lists:

  • Permits are needed to add on, demolish, change occupancy, move doors and windows, repair fire damage or install a fence.
  • Fireplaces, woodstoves and heat-producing devices also need permits.
  • Ordinary repairs, siding, roofing over no more than two layers, and windows or doors of equal size need no permit.
  • A permit lasts 12 months from issue.

Plan review for a new dwelling can run two to six weeks, so settle an unpermitted addition before you list. A direct buyer will often take a house with open permit questions, which a lender-backed buyer may not.

Recording a deed in Onondaga County

Deeds for Cicero parcels are recorded by the Onondaga County Clerk. The base fee for a deed is $45.50 plus $5 per page, and transfer tax is $4 per thousand dollars of price. A TP-584 return costs $5, the RP-5217 form costs $125 for improved residential or agricultural property and $250 for improved commercial property or vacant land, and a $10 charge applies to residential deeds.

State law puts the base transfer tax on the seller, at $2 for every $500 of price, and the TP-584 is due within 15 days of the deed. Recording is also where a mansion tax of 1 percent attaches to residences at $1 million or more, paid by the buyer.

If you are timing a closing, note that the clerk's office closes every first Tuesday of the month from 10:30 to 11:00 a.m. for a staff meeting.

Selling a Cicero house as is

Cicero sellers can list with an agent, sell on their own, or sell directly to a company like ours. Cash buyers pay little attention to a worn roof or a dated kitchen, and the sale does not depend on a lender's appraisal. You still need a clear title, the tax bills in order and a deed ready to record, and the closing attorney coordinates those pieces.

Before you ask for offers, collect the deed, the latest town and school bills, any permit papers for past work and a payoff statement for each loan. With those in hand the buyer can name a price quickly, and the attorney can order the title search the same week.

The next Board of Assessment Review date posted by the town is Tuesday, May 25, 2027. Complaints must be in by 3:00 p.m. that day, and hearings are by appointment.

Pay the Cicero Receiver of Taxes at Town Hall, 8236 Brewerton Road, Cicero, NY 13039. The office collects town, county, village and school taxes for parcels in town.

Can I sell a Cicero house that has unpermitted work?

You can sell it, but the town cannot issue a Certificate of Occupancy or Compliance for work done without a permit. Call Zoning and Planning to learn what the town would require.

What does the county charge to record a deed in Onondaga County?

The base fee is $45.50 plus $5 per page, with $5 for the TP-584 and $125 for the RP-5217 on residential property. Transfer tax is $4 per thousand dollars of price.

Owners live in 86.4 percent of homes, so very few are rented. Nearly every sale involves a homeowner with built-up equity and a buyer moving into the district. Investor-owned houses are a small niche.

School reputation is a main selling point. The Pittsford Central School District runs the Sutherland and Mendon high schools, the Barker Road and Calkins Road middle schools, and five elementary schools: Jefferson, Park, Thornell, Mendon Center and Allen Creek. Buyers sometimes ask for the attendance zone of a particular address, so ask the district office to confirm the school assignment before you quote it in a listing.

What does the assessor's calendar look like in Pittsford?

Pittsford assesses at full value and follows the state calendar. The valuation date is July 1 of the previous year, and the taxable status date is March 1, when all exemption forms must be on file. Informal reviews run from July 1 to March 1, any change is mailed between May 1 and May 15, and the formal review falls on the fourth Tuesday in May, which will be May 25, 2027. The Assessment Review Board has five members and meets once a year.

Exemptions the Assessor's Office handles include:

  • Senior Citizens with Limited Income, capped at $58,400 for town and county and $37,400 for school.
  • Disability with Limited Income, with the same caps.
  • Alternative and Cold War Veteran exemptions.

New STAR applicants register with the State and receive a credit check instead of an exemption on the school bill. The assessor can be reached at (585) 248-6230.

Code and zoning rules

Pittsford requires building permits for construction, additions, alterations and demolition, pools, signs, sheds, decks, basement finishing and generators. After a permit is issued and the work meets zoning, a certificate of occupancy is issued. The Design Review and Historic Preservation Board reviews architectural plans for new structures and renovations, and the Zoning Board of Appeals hears variance requests.

Two other points matter to sellers. Sewer service reaches about 70 percent of the town, so the rest use septic systems, and a buyer will probably want a septic inspection. Whatever is owed is normally paid from your proceeds at closing. Knowing the figure early lets you compare offers on what you will actually receive. If the sale happens between bills, ask your attorney how the current year's taxes will be split between you and the buyer.

What a cash sale skips and what it keeps

A cash buyer skips the mortgage lender's appraisal and underwriting, which is where many financed sales slow down or fall apart. A house with an old roof, a failing septic system or an unfinished project may not satisfy a lender, and cash avoids that problem.

The rest of the sale stays the same. Title still has to be searched, the deed still has to be signed and recorded, and permits, certificates of occupancy and tax balances still matter. Ask for any offer in writing, find out who pays each closing cost, and have an attorney read the contract before you sign. The more of your paperwork is ready, the shorter the path from offer to closing.

Is my Pittsford house in the village?

The village of Pittsford sits in the middle of the town along routes 96 and 31. A house inside it may carry village charges on top of town ones, so confirm the location of your parcel. The Monroe County Real Property Portal shows tax parcel records, and the Pittsford Assessor's Office can confirm specific parcels.

Delinquent taxes can lead to county foreclosure and a public auction of the parcel, and that reaches parcels in Pittsford, including the village. Anyone behind on taxes should call the County Treasury before listing.

October 1, with full payment accepted at Town Hall through October 31 with 2 percent interest. From November 1 through 18 only the Monroe County Treasury takes payment, with 5 percent interest, and nothing is accepted after November 18.

The fourth Tuesday in May, which is May 25 in 2027. The Assessment Review Board has five members and meets once a year.

About 70 percent of the town is on community sewer service. Properties outside those areas use private septic systems, which a buyer will likely want inspected.

The Code Enforcement and Building Department at Town Hall, 11 South Main Street, at (585) 248-6265. It issues permits and the certificates of occupancy and compliance.

Selling fast in Middletown

In Middletown the fastest exit is a straight sale to a cash buyer, because no lender, appraiser or repair list holds up the closing. A listing with an agent may bring more money, but only if the place shows well and you can sit through weeks of showings.

Middletown houses run from large Victorians to older two-family buildings to post-war ranches, and condition changes from one block to the next. Appraisers mark down a tired roof or an old kitchen, so fewer mortgage buyers qualify for such a house. As-is purchasers step in where financing falls short.

Start a folder with your deed, the loan payoff figure, the newest city tax bill and any rental permit for a tenant. Buyers and title agents ask for these first, so having them ready trims a week of emails.

Middletown housing at a glance

Middletown has about 30,098 residents and 9,970 households, and owners and renters split almost evenly: 51.7 percent of households own. A typical owner-occupied home is valued at $308,600, while rent runs about $1,661 a month. With rent that strong against the home value, plenty of owners here keep tenants, so the rental rules below can decide whether a deal closes.

The city sits near the junction of I-84 and NY 17, and the average trip to work is 36.0 minutes. Older houses here face hard winters and damp years, so inspectors look first at stained ceilings, wet basements and aging heating systems. A worn roof or a cellar that floods each spring gets priced in by a cash buyer, who then moves on. Someone using a mortgage may insist on the repair first, and that eats weeks.

Rental permits and occupancy

The rental permit is the main item. Chapter 296 of the city code forbids an owner to let anyone live in a single-family house, or an owner-occupied two-family, without a current permit from the Department of Public Works.

  • The application fee is $100 per rental unit. A permit runs two years, or less if the occupant changes.
  • The city inspects before it issues a permit and again each time one tenant leaves and another moves in.
  • A background check on each new tenant must be on file, and the managing agent has to live on site or within ten miles of the city.
  • Renting with no permit draws a fine of $250 to $1,000, and every day counts as its own offense.

Under Chapter 193, nobody may occupy a building that is newly built, enlarged or converted to a new use until the Commissioner of Public Works issues a certificate of occupancy. Selling with a tenant in place? Phone the Department of Public Works and verify the permit before signing anything. An expired one tends to appear late in a mortgage sale and freeze it.

Tax rates and due dates

One bill covers city, county and library tax, and you can pay it in two halves. Each half carries its own deadline and late charge.

Neglected houses carry one more risk. A local law in effect since 2024 lets the city add unpaid charges for tall grass, snow removal, garbage cans, bulk pickup, dead trees and demolition to the property tax bill. Clear any open charges at the Finance Office ahead of closing.

Assessments, exemptions and grievances

March 1 opens the assessment calendar and doubles as the taxable status date and exemption deadline. The tentative roll comes out May 1, Grievance Day is the fourth Tuesday of May, and the final roll lands July 1.

Think the assessment runs high? File before Grievance Day and attach evidence, for example recent sales of similar houses or repair estimates. The Assessor reviews every transfer for buyer, seller and price, so your contract price will be visible to the city.

If you sell partway through the year, ask the Assessor what exemptions the parcel carries. Whoever buys has to apply for theirs by March 1.

Recording the deed in Orange County

Deeds are recorded by the Orange County Clerk. A residential filing pays $125 for the RP-5217 and a flat $45 that covers the recording page, then adds a per-page charge of $5, a $5 TP-584 fee and a $10 state deed fraud letter.

The clerk accepts cash, check or money order, made out to the Orange County Clerk. A personal check cannot exceed $250, and the counter takes no cards. The deed needs original signatures with a notary's acknowledgment. Clerks check the form against recording requirements but do not judge whether it is legally sufficient.

The seller pays the base transfer tax, and its return is due by the 15th day after the deed is handed over. Surcharges written for New York City do not reach a Middletown closing. Your closing attorney or title agent normally files all of this, so ask them to confirm the amounts before the closing date.

What a cash sale skips

With cash there is no lender in the chain, so appraisal, underwriting and lender repair demands all disappear. You can often choose the closing date, sometimes only a few weeks out. You still need clear title, a valid rental permit if the house has a tenant, and no open city charges on the tax bill. Sort those out first and the sale can move as fast as you want it to.

A simple order of work helps. Pull the rental permit and tax bill first, since those come from city offices. Then ask your attorney for the payoff letter and a title search. Walk through the house and list anything an inspector would flag, such as a leaking roof or an old boiler, so you can tell each buyer about it up front. Offers that already account for the condition rarely get renegotiated at the closing table.

On closing day, expect to sign the deed before a notary, hand over keys, and settle the payoff with your lender. If a second tax half is still unpaid when you close, ask your attorney to have it paid from the proceeds so the buyer starts clean. Keep copies of every document you sign and of the final closing statement for your own tax records.

Frequently asked questions

Can a Middletown house with tenants be sold?

Yes, provided the rental permit is current. The city requires one for single-family and owner-occupied two-family rentals. Call the Department of Public Works to check the status before taking an offer.

What is the combined Middletown tax rate?

It is $129.75 per $1,000 of assessed value as of January 1, 2026, made up of $100.4323 city, $22.890301 county and $6.426390 library. Bills fall due March 1 and July 1.

What date is Grievance Day in Middletown?

It lands on the fourth Tuesday in May, after the May 1 tentative roll. Exemption applications close March 1.

What does the Orange County Clerk charge to record a deed?

A residential deed costs a flat $45 plus $5 per page, with separate charges for the TP-584, the deed fraud letter and the $125 RP-5217, and transfer tax on top. Ask your attorney to confirm the total before filing.

Are New York City transfer taxes charged on a Middletown sale?

No, those taxes apply to conveyances inside New York City. A Middletown seller pays the standard state rate of $2 per $500.

Homeowners here can hire an agent, go it alone, or take a direct cash purchase, and condition plus patience usually decide. Check first that you are in the city proper. The 14120 ZIP code also reaches southern parts of the towns of Wheatfield and Pendleton.

Niagara County's second-largest city after Niagara Falls, North Tonawanda lies between the Niagara River on the west and Tonawanda Creek and the Erie Canal on the south. It has 29,806 residents, 2.3% fewer than in 2020.

  • Typical owner-occupied home value: $197,200
  • Share of homes lived in by owners: 70.1%
  • Median gross rent: $934 a month
  • Median household income: $66,961

Across 14,015 households of about 2.14 people, long-time owners dominate. Roughly 91% of residents stayed in the same house for a year, so listings are not constant.

Homes built in the Lumber City

Local pride runs to the nickname Lumber City, and the housing grew from that trade. From the mid-19th century into the 1970s it was a lumber forwarding center, and more than 150 lumber companies operated here. The Ray H. Bennett Lumber Company sold kit homes across the United States and Canada for about 70 years, so an older house on your block may be a kit home, a detail some buyers like to hear. Goundry Street has mansions built for lumber barons.

Location sells here too. Downtown draws buyers who like the Riviera Theatre on Webster Street, the City Market, Gateway Harbor Park on the canal, and Gratwick-Riverside Park, a 53-acre park on the Niagara River.

Rental registration

Under Chapter 51D of the city code, every owner of rental property in North Tonawanda registers each rental unit with the Building Department, and owner-occupied properties register too, without a fee.

A certificate lasts up to one year or until ownership changes, which means a rental's new owner registers separately once the deed transfers. Registering consents to inspection by Code Enforcement for compliance with the city chapter and the New York State building and fire codes.

  • Applicants submit photo identification.
  • An owner who does not live in Niagara County, Erie, Genesee or Orleans County must name a property manager who does, and who can accept legal notices.
  • A first conviction for failing to register carries a fine of $250 to $500. A second within twelve months carries $500 to $2,500.
  • A fine unpaid after 30 days becomes a lien on the property and is collected like a tax.

A rental owner who sells without a current registration invites trouble, so landlords should fix any registration gap before selling, because a lien shows up in a title search. Visit the Building Department at 216 Payne Avenue or call (716) 692-2680.

Assessment grievances and exemptions

Every year Grievance Day falls on the fourth Tuesday in May, and forms are at the Assessor's office from March. Use the online property search to open any parcel, choose Additional Info, then View Tax Detail, for a year by year tax summary.

Buyers ask about exemptions, so keep these basics handy:

  • Basic STAR requires owning and living in the home with income of $500,000 or less.
  • Enhanced STAR requires age 65 and adjusted gross income of $110,750 or less.
  • People who bought after 2015 sign up with the state for the STAR Credit.
  • The low-income senior exemption has an income limit of $34,400, and the disability exemption has a limit of $34,600.
  • Military service exemptions are capped for assessments above $120,000.

A free copy of your deed is available from the Assessor on request, handy when you assemble closing papers. Details at 695-8597.

Deeds, transfer tax and city water

North Tonawanda deeds are recorded by the Niagara County Clerk and not at City Hall. Call the recording office at (716) 439-7022; it is open weekdays from 9:30 AM to 4:30 PM.

Filing takes a signed original deed, a TP-584 transfer tax return and an RP-5217 real property transfer report. The seller pays the state transfer tax of $2 for each $500, or $4 per $1,000, due within 15 days after the deed is delivered. A closing attorney or title company normally handles this for you.

Before closing, settle city water. After two consecutive estimated water meter readings, a $25 fee applies each quarter until the meter is read, and readings can be dropped off or submitted online. Ask the Treasurer's office at (716) 695-8575 for the current balance and how it is handled at transfer.

Schools, roads and weather

One city school district covers North Tonawanda, and the average commute is 20.4 minutes, short enough to put in the listing. Precipitation falls on about 171 days a year and snow on about 57, so roof, gutter and basement condition deserve a close look before you list.

Sell as-isNo repairs, no cleaning and no showings. We buy North Tonawanda houses in any condition.See My Cash Offer →

What buyers ask about a North Tonawanda house

Buyers tend to raise the same four topics. First, age and condition: with snow on about 57 days a year, buyers look hard at roofs, gutters and basements. Second, any rental history and whether the registration is current. Third, the water meter and whether a balance is open. Fourth, which exemptions the house now carries, since a buyer must apply for their own. Written answers shorten negotiations. Direct buyers usually ask fewer questions, though a clean file still helps your price. If you sell as-is, say so in the first conversation, list the known problems, and let the offer reflect them. That keeps the number from changing after an inspection.

Getting the file ready

Give yourself a few weeks of lead time. Assemble the deed, your latest tax and water statements and a lender payoff letter, in one folder so that nothing is hunted for later. If the house is a rental, confirm the registration with the Building Department first. Your attorney can name the forms the sale needs, and the Assessor will hand over the deed copy at no charge. A cash buyer can take the house as it stands, which spares you showings and repair credits, and closing follows your own calendar once the title work is done.

Ask the Treasurer for the water balance a few days before closing so no surprise reaches the table. At the closing you sign the deed and the transfer tax forms, the mortgage is paid, and the clerk records the deed. If you were a landlord, remember that the buyer registers the units in their own name afterward.

Frequently asked questions

Can I sell a rental house in North Tonawanda if it is not registered?

Register it before the sale. Failing to register is a violation with fines of $250 to $500 for a first conviction, and an unpaid fine becomes a lien on the property.

Where do I file a deed after selling in North Tonawanda?

File it with the Niagara County Clerk. The seller pays transfer tax of $2 per $500, and the TP-584 and RP-5217 forms go in with the deed.

When is Grievance Day in North Tonawanda?

It is always the fourth Tuesday in May. Grievance forms are available from the Assessor's office starting in March.

Is a 14120 mailing address always inside North Tonawanda city limits?

No. The ZIP code 14120 also covers southern parts of the towns of Wheatfield and Pendleton, so check your tax bill to see which municipality governs your house.

What happens to my rental registration when I sell?

The certificate lasts up to one year or until ownership changes. After the sale the new owner registers the units with the Building Department.

Town, village and hamlets

Orchard Park is a town with a village inside it. The town covers 38.52 square miles about 14 miles southeast of downtown Buffalo, so the first question is whether your lot lies in the village or out in the town. The area broke from Hamburg in 1850, was named Ellicott and then East Hamburgh, and became Orchard Park on March 1, 1934.

Hamlets within the town limits include Armor, Duells Corner, Ellicott, Loveland and Webster Corners. Highmark Stadium stands in the hamlet of Windom at the town's western edge, while Chestnut Ridge Park, the largest park in Erie County, anchors the south. US 219 follows the west side, US 20 across the north, and NY 277 and NY 240 meet near US 20.

Showings turn to schools quickly. Orchard Park Central School District has four K-5 buildings (Eggert, Ellicott, South Davis and Windom), one middle school and one high school. Put the correct elementary school in your listing and buyers have one less thing to ask.

Local housing numbers

The town had 29,804 residents in mid-2025, living in 12,829 households. Homeowners live in 74.5 percent of the housing, the typical owned home is valued at $360,700, and median rent is $1,304 a month. Monthly owner costs have a median of $2,323 with a mortgage and $910 without.

Households rarely move: 91.6 percent of residents were at the same address a year earlier. With few houses changing hands, a well-prepared one gets noticed, so tidy presentation and clean paperwork count.

Which Orchard Park offices handle permits, assessments and recording?

Four offices touch almost every part of a sale.

  • Assessor's Office: keeps your assessment, takes informal review requests and receives grievance paperwork. Phone 716-662-6420.
  • Building Inspector and Code Enforcement: permits, inspections and zoning verification letters, from the Municipal Center on South Buffalo Street in the village. Weekday lunch closure at the counter runs 1 PM to 2 PM.
  • Town Board: holds meetings in the Municipal Building courtroom on the first and third Wednesdays monthly.
  • Erie County Clerk: files the deed and takes in the transfer tax.

The town has been reviewing rezoning near the stadium along with zoning map amendments. Own a parcel by the stadium or on a corridor under study? Ask the building office for a zoning verification letter before pricing the house.

Contesting your assessment

You can contest an assessment only in the spring, around Grievance Day on the fourth Tuesday of May. The Assessor's Office works from the calendar below and reports a 1990 revaluation, a uniform level of assessment of 28.5 percent and 12,412 parcels.

At 28.5 percent, the assessed value printed on your notice is well under market value, so it is not a price. Hearing requests are due before Grievance Day. Hearings run from 4 PM to 8 PM in the Town Hall basement meeting room, and email or upload submissions are not accepted. Bring Form RP-524 and supporting documents, with copies for each of the five review board members. Phone the assessor for this year's schedule, and read the assessment review page first.

Village houses may have a second assessment, since villages that assess property accept their own RP-524 complaints. Ask whether yours is one.

Transfer tax and recording fees

Sellers here pay one combined transfer tax: $4.50 for each $500 of price, with any leftover fraction rounded up to a full $500. New York gets $2.00 and Erie County gets $2.50, collected by the clerk as the deed is filed. A seller who is 62 or older and has lived in a one or two family home for at least a year can sign an affidavit, free at the clerk's office, to pay only $2.00 per $500.

Recording is billed separately. On the clerk's residential deed schedule the statutory fee is $45, every written side of a page adds $5, Form TP-584 is $10 and the RP-5217 transfer report is $125, which puts a three-page deed at $195. A 1 percent mansion tax applies from $1 million up, paid by the buyer.

Paperwork that can slow a closing

Start with the state's seller questionnaire. Real Property Law 462 has the owner of a house with up to four units sign it and deliver it ahead of the buyer's signature on the contract. An as-is clause is still allowed. Several questions line up with local houses:

  • Are there certificates of occupancy for the building?
  • Is the water municipal or from a well, and does waste go to a public sewer or a septic tank?
  • Has the lot had flooding, drainage trouble or water in the structure?
  • What school district is the address in?

Starting work before the permit is issued means paying a double fee. The permit list includes decks, fences, sheds, pools, roofing, furnace and air conditioning replacements, generators and added plumbing fixtures, and the town has asked for plumbing permits on all plumbing work since January 2020. Owners must also clear snow and ice from sidewalks beside their land. Close out or disclose any gap before an inspector or buyer spots it.

When does a cash purchase suit an Orchard Park owner?

No lender means no appraisal or loan approval to wait on, leaving title work, state forms and recording. Cash appeals to owners who want to avoid showings and repairs, such as heirs to a house or people moving on a set date.

On any route, start by collecting your tax bill, permit records for earlier work and the Erie County deed details. Keep offers in writing, decide who pays each closing cost, and have a New York attorney review the contract before signing. Expect the disclosure form, the transfer tax and any lien payoff to land on you as seller. Ask the title company for a payoff letter from any lender so the figure is ready when the closing date is set.

A simple order of work helps. First, check with the building office for open permits. Second, read the seller questionnaire and answer it. Third, ask the Assessor's Office whether your house is in the village or the town, since that decides which assessment applies. Fourth, line up an attorney. Doing these before you accept an offer keeps the closing from stalling on small items, and a cash buyer with a fixed date will expect them done.

Frequently asked questions

Does the buyer or the seller cover Orchard Park's transfer tax?

The seller pays. Erie County's combined rate is $4.50 per $500, made up of $2.00 for the state and $2.50 for the county. A qualifying seller aged 62 or older may pay the reduced $2.00 rate.

Can I sell an Orchard Park house that needs repairs?

Yes, because both sides may agree to sell as-is. The signed seller questionnaire still goes to the buyer first, so answer honestly from what you know.

When is Grievance Day in Orchard Park?

It is the fourth Tuesday of May. The Assessor's Office can confirm the exact date, the appointment deadline and how many copies of the complaint form to bring.

What should I do about unpermitted work on my Orchard Park house?

Talk to the building office before listing. A late permit costs a double fee, and the state questionnaire asks about certificates of occupancy. Resolving it now beats renegotiating a contract later.

Which office records an Orchard Park deed?

The Erie County Clerk, who also collects the transfer tax at the same visit. A three-page residential deed costs $195 to record. Your attorney or title company usually files it.

Three local items tend to come up in any sale: the septic inspection rule, flood questions and the Building Department's permit records. Each is easier to settle before a buyer asks.

East Fishkill sits on the southern edge of Dutchess County and covers 56.53 square miles. Hamlets include Arthursburg, Fishkill Plains, Gayhead, Hopewell Junction, Peckslip and Stormville. Interstate 84 and the Taconic State Parkway both cross the town. Population is 29,801.

Most owners stay put, so gather the latest closed sales near your own street, not just a town figure. Describe highway access plainly in a listing, since the average commute is long.

School districts

Four districts reach into town: Arlington, Carmel, Pawling and Wappingers Central School Districts. The town's Receiver of Taxes collects school taxes for two of them, Wappingers and Carmel.

The district decides the school tax bill and its payment calendar, so read the property's current bill before you describe the house to a buyer. The next section shows how the dates differ.

Tax due dates and penalties

County and town taxes are payable once a year, in January and February without penalty. The Receiver of Taxes works from 2464 Route 52 in Hopewell Junction, next to the police station, and also collects fire, lighting and park district charges.

The books close on May 31, and unpaid balances move to the Dutchess County Commissioner of Finance about June 15.

School bills run on a different clock. Wappingers taxes are payable from mid-September into October, with a 2 percent penalty through the end of that month. Carmel taxes are payable in September, and that district alone allows a half payment with a 5 percent charge on each half. Unpaid school taxes are added to the next county and town bill.

Assessments, grievances and exemptions

The assessor values each parcel so school, county, town and special district taxes can be divided fairly, but the assessor does not set the tax rate. The calendar is short: taxable status date on March 1, tentative roll by May 1, Grievance Day on the 4th Tuesday of May, and the final roll on July 1, which is the roll that next year's taxes are based on.

Exemptions for seniors, firefighters and people with disabilities must be filed by March 1. STAR is filed directly with New York State, and the town asks residents not to call its office about it. Only the current tentative roll can be grieved, so a seller who thinks the value is wrong should raise it before the May hearing.

Septic, flood and water items

Three local rules can surface during a sale, and each is easier to handle before a buyer asks.

  • Septic: owners inside the East of Hudson Watershed must have each system pumped, cleaned and visually inspected by a registered water transporter at least every five years, and file the inspection form with the Building Department.
  • Flood: East Fishkill joined FEMA's Community Rating System in October 2015 as a Class 8 community, giving a 10 percent premium discount inside the Special Flood Hazard Area and 5 percent outside it. Homeowner policies do not pay flood losses, and a new flood policy has a five-day waiting period.
  • Water and sewer: the town runs 17 water districts and 6 sewer districts, billed every three months, with a 10 percent late fee after the first month and unpaid rents re-levied on the next tax bill after November 1.

Dutchess County's Parcel Access map can show whether a property lies in a flood area, and the Building Department can supply flood data to sellers and lenders.

Permits and certificates

The Building Department's process starts with a complete general permit application, then a pre-site inspection, plan review, permit issuance, inspections called in by the contractor, and a final certificate once the last inspection passes. A certificate of occupancy fee applies where relevant, and the town offers an online permit portal.

If you added a deck, finished a basement or built a garage, find the final certificate before you list. The Building Department sits on the lower level of Town Hall, with the entrance at the rear, and also houses the zoning officer and floodplain administrator.

Recording a deed

Recording a deed with the Dutchess County Clerk costs $45, plus $5 per page, $5 for the capital gains affidavit that accompanies form TP-584, and a $10 residential deed notification fee. State transfer tax of two dollars per $500 of price is separate and goes in with the return within 15 days of delivery.

Your closing attorney can total these and confirm what applies to your deed.

Steps for a quick sale

Pull together your latest county and town and school bills, the septic inspection form if you are in the watershed, any flood policy, and the permit certificates for work done. Then ask for offers and compare each with what you owe. A cash buyer will usually take the house as it stands, which spares you repairs and showings.

Closing day brings payoffs from your proceeds, delivery of the deed, and the transfer tax return within 15 days. Ask the Receiver of Taxes for a payoff on any open bill, since balances left after May 31 move to the Dutchess County Commissioner of Finance.

If the house is inside the East of Hudson Watershed, have the septic pumped and inspected before you list and file the form with the Building Department, so a buyer sees a finished record. If you are not sure whether a flood policy is needed, check the county's Parcel Access map and keep the result with your sale papers. Water and sewer rents are billed every three months, so ask the town for a current balance before closing.

Yes. East Fishkill sits on the southern border of Dutchess County and became its own town on November 29, 1849. Its tax office is on Route 52 in Hopewell Junction.

The middle value for owner-occupied homes is $478,400 for 2020 to 2024. That is a survey figure, so recent sales on your own street are the better guide to a price.

When is the last day to pay county and town taxes without a penalty?

February 28. A 2 percent charge applies in March, 3 percent in April, and 4 percent plus $2 in May, after which the county takes over collection.

Do East Fishkill septic systems need inspections before a sale?

Systems inside the East of Hudson Watershed must be pumped and inspected at least once every five years under the Town Code. Ask the Building Department whether your property lies in the watershed area.

Who sets property assessments in East Fishkill?

The Town Assessor values each property, and Grievance Day is the 4th Tuesday in May. The assessor cannot change the tax rate, which comes from the school, county, town and district budgets.

Building rules and permits

Plan on about 10 days for most permit reviews. Built a deck or finished a basement without a permit? Ask the department what it needs before you list, since the buyer's attorney may bring it up at contract.

The collection window runs through April with a penalty each month: 1.25 percent in February, 2.5 percent in March and 3.75 percent in April. On May 1 the unpaid balance moves to the Schenectady County Commissioner of Finance.

School bills arrive around September 1, stay penalty-free through September, and go to the county on November 1 when unpaid. Whatever remains, penalties included, joins the next January town and county bill, so a missed school payment can hit a bill the buyer expects to be clean. Water rent bills go out by June 1, and unpaid water charges are also carried onto the following January bill.

County and town general charges apply to every parcel in town. Town outside, highway and some other lines apply only to parcels outside the village. Fire district and special district charges depend on the street. A house in Scotia also receives a separate village bill, due in June.

Assessment grievances and exemptions

A lower assessment helps only if you file before Grievance Day, which in Glenville is the fourth Tuesday in May. Use the state RP-524 complaint form for the challenge.

The Assessor's Office also handles exemptions for low-income seniors, volunteer firefighters and ambulance workers, plus the STAR program. If you receive STAR on the house, tell your closing attorney, because the benefit is tied to the owner. A seller should close the STAR registration after a sale, and a new owner registers once the house becomes their primary home.

Water and sewer at closing

Glenville runs an online request just for sellers. The Public Works water and sewer pages include a Closing Adjustment Request form, and the form asks you to allow 48 hours for the water or sewer closing adjustment to be forwarded to the closing contact. File it as soon as you have a contract date so the buyer's attorney is not waiting on a meter reading.

If the house is on a private well or septic system rather than town service, the disclosure statement still asks about water source, water testing, sewage type, and the date a septic tank was last pumped. A cash buyer will usually ask for the same details.

Recording the deed

The deed is recorded with the Schenectady County Clerk, and the county then passes the ownership change to the town for data entry. The paperwork follows New York's standard package: form TP-584 and the Real Property Transfer Report RP-5217, plus state transfer tax of $2 for each $500 of price. Fees differ by county, so ask the Schenectady County Clerk for its current schedule, or ask your closing attorney to quote the total.

  • Confirm the legal owners on the deed match the people signing the contract.
  • Collect any open permit paperwork before the attorney orders the title search.
  • Ask the attorney for the final figure for transfer tax and recording fees in writing.

Comparing offers

  • The net amount after taxes, payoffs, water charges and recording costs, not just the headline price.
  • Whether the buyer takes the house as is, or asks you to complete repairs after inspection.
  • The closing date, and who covers any gap between contract and closing.
  • Proof of funds, if the offer is cash.
  • Any condition tied to the disclosure statement or a title problem.

Frequently asked questions

Can I sell a Glenville house without making repairs first?

Yes. New York law lets a seller and buyer agree to an as-is sale, but you must still give the buyer a signed property condition disclosure statement before the buyer signs a binding contract. Expect an as-is price below a repaired, staged listing.

Who do I pay property taxes to in Glenville?

Town and county bills are paid to the Glenville Receiver of Taxes in January, with monthly penalties through April. School bills are collected in September, and unpaid bills later move to the Schenectady County Commissioner of Finance.

Does a Scotia address change anything about the sale?

It can. Houses inside the Village of Scotia receive a village tax bill due in June, and the village may have its own building office. Houses elsewhere in Glenville do not get that bill.

How do I get the water and sewer figures for my closing?

Submit the closing adjustment request on the town's Public Works water and sewer pages and allow 48 hours. The result goes to the closing contact you name on the form.

When is Grievance Day in Glenville?

The fourth Tuesday in May. File the state RP-524 form before then if you think your assessment is too high.

Selling in East Hampton: the main routes

East Hampton sellers can put the house on the market, sell privately, or accept a cash purchase. Cash helps most when a certificate of occupancy is unresolved, repairs were postponed, or a tenant is living there, since cash buyers often take a property as it stands.

Start with the permit file, any rental registry paperwork and your latest tax bills. If the house is rented, update the registry whenever the tenancy changes so the town's record matches who lives there. Then weigh a quick close against the higher price a full market sale might bring. A sale that depends on a new certificate should leave room in the schedule, because the Building Department has a backlog.

The town and its housing

East Hampton is the easternmost town in New York, at the far end of Long Island's South Fork in Suffolk County. It covers 74.33 square miles and includes the village of East Hampton, part of the village of Sag Harbor, and hamlets such as Montauk, Amagansett, Wainscott, Springs, Northwest Harbor and Napeague. Water borders it on several sides, so a house in Montauk and a house in Springs reach very different buyers. Montauk is New York's largest fishing port, and summer crowds still drive much of the economy, which shapes who shops for a house there and when.

Population is 29,400. About 77.8 percent of homes are lived in by their owners, and the typical value of those homes is $1,178,500. Typical household income is $132,348 and typical monthly rent is $2,578. With values this high, many sales pass the $1 million line where the state adds a residential tax for buyers, so look at price and closing figures carefully with your attorney.

Property tax bills

The Receiver of Taxes prepares more than 24,000 bills and distributes the money to Suffolk County, the town, nine fire and fire protection districts, six school districts with five libraries and one museum district, five lighting districts, five road and water connection districts, and special use districts.

Each collection season ends on June 1, and the online payment portal closes the next day. After that, payments with penalties and interest go to the Suffolk County Comptroller in Riverhead. The portal still lets you view and print bills and receipts. The town recommends certified mail with your tax map number if you pay late.

Certificate of occupancy on a sale

The Town Code requires an updated certificate of occupancy on any change of ownership, with two exceptions. Under Chapter 102-14, no new certificate is needed if one was issued within six months before the transfer, or if the transfer only moves the property to a trust, LLC or similar entity for estate planning with the same beneficial owner.

The Town Board paused enforcement on March 10, 2026, and the pause runs retroactively from January 1, 2024 through December 31, 2026. The Building Department still processes applications, and it tells sellers to keep applying. Roughly six in ten applications involve improvements built without a permit, which lengthens review.

Building applications and zoning limits

Every Building Department application must be filed digitally through the town's OpenGov portal, and payments are made online, not at the counter. Counter drop-off runs 8:30 am to 3:30 pm on weekdays, with the first half hour reserved for contractors and 9:00 to 10:30 am for the general public.

A zoning amendment effective July 1, 2025 limits gross floor area for a single-family residence to 7 percent of lot area plus 1,500 square feet or 10,000 square feet, whichever is less. Any building permit that includes clearing needs a staked survey showing the clearing envelope. If the house is rented, the rental registry requires a signed, notarized update form every time the tenancy changes.

Community Preservation Fund tax

The Peconic Bay Community Preservation Fund is financed by a 2 percent real estate transfer tax, created by Town Law 64-e in 1998 and administered under Tax Law section 31-d. A 2024 State Comptroller audit reported $127.2 million deposited during 2021 and 2022 and 2,352 acres of open space, farmland, parks and historic sites preserved through the end of 2022.

Ask your closing attorney whether the tax applies to your sale, which side pays it, and whether an exemption fits. The state also charges $2 per $500 of price through the TP-584 return, plus an extra 1 percent on residences at $1 million or more.

Selling a rented house

A tenant in place complicates a sale in two ways. First, the town's rental registry needs a signed, notarized update form every time the tenancy changes, and a sale that ends a tenancy is a change. Second, a buyer will want to know whether the rental was ever permitted. Open building permits tied to the rental must be closed out, or renewal fees and violations can follow.

Pull the registry record and the permit history together before an offer arrives. A cash buyer will often take a tenant-occupied house as it stands, but the price will reflect the open questions, so the cleaner your file, the stronger your number.

Steps to a quick sale

Gather the certificate of occupancy status, the rental registry form if you have a tenant, and the latest tax bills before you talk to any buyer. Then request offers and compare them with what you owe. A cash sale cuts out financing delays and showings. It does not cut out the certificate question, the Community Preservation Fund tax, or the transfer tax return, so ask your attorney who handles each one.

Closing day brings payoffs from your proceeds, delivery of the deed, and the state filings that follow.

Is East Hampton a town or a village?

Both exist. The Town of East Hampton is the large municipality of 74.33 square miles, and the incorporated village of East Hampton sits inside it, along with part of Sag Harbor and several hamlets.

What is the typical home value in East Hampton?

Roughly $1,178,500 for homes occupied by their owners. Household income in the middle of the range is $132,348.

Do I need an updated certificate of occupancy to sell in East Hampton?

The code requires one when ownership changes, though enforcement is paused through December 31, 2026. The Building Department still takes applications, charges $600, and advises sellers to apply.

When is Grievance Day in East Hampton?

The third Tuesday in May. The tentative roll is posted May 1, and the final roll arrives July 1.

Who do I pay if I missed the East Hampton tax deadline?

After June 1 the Town no longer accepts payment. Late payments, with penalties and interest, go to the Suffolk County Comptroller.

What speeds up a house sale in Queensbury?

Knowing the tax calendar and the permit history before a buyer asks, then choosing a buyer whose closing does not depend on a lender. A cash purchase skips appraisal and underwriting, while the deed and town records follow the usual path.

Queensbury is a first-class town in Warren County, in the southern Adirondack foothills. It covers 62.80 square miles of land and wraps the city of Glens Falls on three sides. A house here might sit near Lake George, in West Glens Falls or on a rural road, and the school district and fire district on your bills depend on where it is.

Districts and local services

Four school districts cover the town: Queensbury Union Free, Glens Falls City, Hudson Falls Central and Lake George Central. Your school tax bill names yours, and a listing should too, since buyers ask about it first.

Five fire protection districts operate here: Bay Ridge, North Queensbury, Queensbury Central, South Queensbury and West Glens Falls. Hamlets include Glen Lake, West Glens Falls, Kattskill Bay, East Lake George, Oneida Corners and Harrisena.

Lake George forms the northern edge of town and the Hudson River runs along the southern boundary. Parts of the western and northern town fall inside the Adirondack Park, which can add permit conditions to a parcel. The town has had no police force of its own since 1982, so the Warren County Sheriff's Office and the State Police cover it.

Queensbury housing at a glance

Queensbury leans toward ownership and toward older residents. Owners live in 75.5% of the homes, and 25.9% of residents are 65 or older. With a population of 29,049, the town is steady rather than growing fast.

Buildings and Codes before a sale

The Town of Queensbury's Buildings and Codes office is where you ask about permits and certificates of occupancy. The planning and zoning offices handle land use questions.

Ask whether your house has a certificate of occupancy on file for every addition, whether any permits are still open, and whether the town expects any inspection or certificate in connection with the transfer. Put these questions to the office early. A missing certificate for a finished attic or garage conversion is the kind of gap that delays a closing.

A house on septic raises more questions. New York's disclosure form asks for the system's age, the date of the last pumping and how often it is pumped, so dig those records out before listing. The same form covers flood zones, wetlands, agricultural districts and fuel tanks, all common on lakeside or rural lots.

Property tax calendar and assessments

Warren County's Real Property Tax Services publishes the yearly calendar Queensbury follows. Around September 1 most school district bills go out, and around January 1 most municipal bills do, each with 30 days free of interest. New purchasers are told to contact both the school and municipal tax collectors so a bill is not missed.

  • March 1: Taxable Status Date and the deadline to file any exemption, new or renewal, with the Assessor.
  • April 1: all outstanding taxes become county liens payable to the county Treasurer.
  • May 1: tentative roll filed and change-of-assessment notices mailed.
  • Fourth Tuesday in May: Grievance Day, when the Board of Assessment Review hears assessment complaints.
  • July 1: assessments become final and are used for the coming year's taxes.

April 1 is the date that surprises sellers. Once a bill has moved to the county, the payoff must come from the county Treasurer rather than the town tax receiver, so have your attorney order the right figure.

Warren County Clerk fees for a deed

The Warren County Clerk records deeds at the municipal center on U.S. Route 9, south of the village of Lake George. The fee schedule lists $40 a document, $5 for the cover sheet, $5 a page, $5 for the TP-584, and $125 for the RP-5217 on qualifying residential or farm property ($250 for other property). Residential deeds also carry a $10 notice of conveyance fee.

State transfer tax is $4.00 per $1,000, with nothing due at $500 or less. Recording and filing are open from 8:00 a.m. until 3:30 p.m., and electronic recording is available. The clerk's office also records Adirondack Park Agency permits, so look for permit conditions on any parcel inside the Park before closing.

What to gather before listing

A short list saves the most time. Pull the school and town tax bills, find any certificates of occupancy, and note when the septic system or well was last serviced. Near Lake George or inside the Adirondack Park, also check recorded documents for easements or permit conditions a buyer will want to see.

Then choose a route. A standard listing reaches owner-occupant buyers but relies on inspections and a mortgage approval. A cash sale closes without a lender. Both end at the county clerk, whose recording window closes at 3:30 p.m., so plan signing times around it.

If taxes are owed when you sell, the closing attorney pays them from the proceeds. After April 1, ask the county Treasurer for the payoff figure rather than the town.

From accepted offer to recorded deed

The order of events is about the same whichever buyer you pick. Once you sign a contract, the buyer's attorney will order title work and ask for the town file: certificates of occupancy, open permits and any septic records. Your attorney requests tax payoff figures from the school and town collectors, or from the county Treasurer once April 1 is behind you.

At closing you sign the deed, the TP-584 transfer tax form and the RP-5217 transfer report. The deed then goes to the Warren County Clerk, where the $4.00 per $1,000 transfer tax is collected with the recording fees. Electronic recording is available, which helps when the filing window is tight.

With a cash buyer the lender steps drop out, so there is no appraisal to wait on and no mortgage commitment that can fall through. The title, tax and permit steps above still apply, which is why gathering those papers first is the most useful thing you can do. If you have an exemption on your bill, remember the buyer must file their own by March 1 to keep one.

Frequently asked questions

How do I tell which school district my Queensbury house is in?

Your school tax bill names it. Four districts share the town: Queensbury Union Free, Glens Falls City, Hudson Falls Central and Lake George Central.

What is the Queensbury tax mailing schedule?

Most school bills are mailed near September 1 and most municipal bills near January 1, each with 30 interest-free days. Anything unpaid becomes a county lien on April 1.

What does recording a Warren County deed cost?

Budget $40 per document plus $5 for the cover sheet, $5 a page, $5 for the TP-584 and $125 for the RP-5217 on qualifying residential property.

Does a parcel inside the Adirondack Park change the sale?

The Warren County Clerk records Adirondack Park Agency permits. Ask whether any permit is recorded against your parcel and give it to the buyer's attorney.

What is Grievance Day in Queensbury?

It falls on the fourth Tuesday in May, when the Board of Assessment Review hears assessment complaints. Exemption filings are due to the Assessor by March 1.

Three routes exist here: hire an agent, sell it yourself, or accept cash from a buyer who takes the house exactly as it is. The town sits in Monroe County next to Rochester, and paperwork flows through Town Hall, the County Clerk and the county's tax portal.

Tidy records make for the quickest sale: a current Compliance Certificate for work done, a tax payoff number, and the correct school district on the bill.

About 91% of residents lived in the same house a year earlier, so many owners have stayed a long time and may be selling a house with original systems. Reassessment and the assessment calendar

The Town of Gates completed a town-wide reassessment in 2025, and the Assessor's page now lists a 2026 final tax assessment roll. The assessed value on a tax bill is therefore recent and tied to current market value.

Assessors weigh each parcel against nearby sales and revise values after a permit reveals new construction, remodeling or demolition. Those figures feed the town, county, school and special district charges, including fire and ambulance. The calendar runs on a fixed cycle:

  • March 1: taxable status date, and the exemption filing deadline.
  • May 1: tentative roll filed and grievance forms become available.
  • Fourth Tuesday in May: Grievance Day before the Board of Assessment Review, which has five resident members.

The Board can only hear valuation complaints, not tax complaints, so check whether the assessed value or an exemption is the problem before you file.

Tax bills and due dates

Two bills arrive each year: Town and County for the calendar year, and school for July 1 to June 30. The Tax Receiver's office is at 1605 Buffalo Road. Collection moves to the Monroe County Treasurer after May 31.

  • Town and County bill: mailed around the turn of the year, with full payment due by February 10 to avoid interest.
  • Late rates: interest begins at 1.5% from February 11 and climbs to 6% by May.
  • School bill: mailed so it arrives in early September, with full payment due by October 1.

Payment at the Receiver's office can be cash, check or card, with a fee on cards. Online bill pay may take up to 14 days and arrive unpostmarked, so start early.

Town services and records

The Town of Gates website carries most of the forms you may need while preparing a sale, and its Town Code is posted online. Browse the code before you list if the house has a shed, fence or other addition that you never checked against the rules.

Permits, compliance certificates and recording

Plans, permits for decks, pools, additions and signs, and Compliance Certificates all come from the Gates Building Department, which also fields zoning questions. A Zoning Compliance Request costs $75. Variance requests go to the Zoning Board of Appeals on the second Monday of the month.

Once you close, the deed is recorded by the Monroe County Clerk at 39 W. Main Street, Room 101 in Rochester. The seller owes the state transfer tax at $2 per $500, and Form TP-584 accompanies the deed. The Monroe County Real Property Portal shows tax bills and sales histories for parcels.

If you owe taxes at sale time

Get a written payoff from the Tax Receiver before picking a closing date. Interest on the Town and County bill begins February 11 and builds monthly to 6% by May, so waiting costs money. After May 31 you will be dealing with the Monroe County Treasurer.

An unpaid balance will not stop a sale. It comes out of your proceeds at the table, and a cash buyer can factor it into the offer. The real problem is finding out late, so call early and keep the answer with your contract papers. Ask also whether the school bill for the year is paid, since that one runs July 1 to June 30 and falls due by October 1, and confirm which district bills the parcel.

Preparing the house and paperwork

Do a short walk-through before you list. Look at the roof, furnace and electrical panel, since owners who have lived in a house for many years often have original systems. If a buyer wants electrical work signed off, the town's list of approved inspectors is the place to start.

Then compare your improvements with the permit printout. A deck, pool or addition without a Compliance Certificate is the kind of gap a buyer's attorney finds. The Building Department can tell you what it needs to close the file.

A cash sale in Gates, step by step

Gather your Compliance Certificates, latest Town and County and school bills, and the permit printout. Share them with the buyer at the first walk-through so the offer reflects what the house is, not what the buyer fears. After you accept, the title search turns up liens or tax balances, and payoffs come out of your proceeds at closing.

Closing includes recording the deed with the Monroe County Clerk and filing the TP-584 return. Because the school and Town and County bills run on different calendars, expect your attorney to prorate whichever one is open on closing day.

Frequently asked questions

What is a Compliance Certificate in Gates?

A document the town Building Department issues after required permits and inspections are complete. Buyers' attorneys often ask for it when a seller added a deck, pool or alteration, so confirm yours is on file.

When is the Gates tax bill due without interest?

Full payment of the Town and County bill is due by February 10. Interest begins on February 11 at 1.5% and rises through May, and payments after May 31 go to the Monroe County Treasurer.

Which school district is my Gates house in?

Gates property falls within either the Gates-Chili Central School District or the Spencerport Central School District. Your tax bill names the district, and the Assessor's Office can confirm it.

At the Monroe County Clerk's office in downtown Rochester, which keeps deeds, mortgages and liens. The office keeps weekday hours from nine to five.

Where Chili sits

Chili is a suburban town in the southwest corner of Monroe County, and its northeastern corner touches the city of Rochester. It covers about 39.9 square miles, almost all of it land. Downtown Rochester is roughly 7 miles northeast of the hamlet of Chili Center. Interstate 490 and the New York State Thruway both cross the town.

The town's own communities are Chili Center, North Chili, South Chili along the Thruway, West Chili near Black Creek Park, and the rural hamlet of Clifton.

Total area39.85 square miles
Population, 2020 census29,123

Median household income$89,793
2025 equalization rate98%

The population was up 1.7 percent from 28,625 in 2010. A median age of 42.9 and a household income of $89,793 point to settled families, and many sellers have owned for years.

School districts and roads

Chili is split among several districts, so the one for your address depends on which part of town you live in. Churchville-Chili, Gates Chili and Wheatland-Chili central school districts all serve the town, and Caledonia-Mumford can apply to a parcel too. Your tax bill's school line settles which district applies, so check it before telling a buyer.

Route numbers get local names here. State Route 33A is Chili Avenue, State Route 386 is the Scottsville-Chili Road, and State Route 252 is Beaver Road. Town Hall is at 3333 Chili Avenue, and the Assessor and the Building Department work from the same building.

  • Interstate 490 is the main highway link toward Rochester.
  • The Thruway (Interstate 90) runs along the rural South Chili area.

How to challenge your Chili assessment

Every property in town is assessed at 100 percent of market value, using a July 1, 2024 valuation date for the current roll. The Assessor sets value and runs exemptions, while the school boards, the County Legislature and the Town Board set the tax rates.

The assessment calendar repeats each year, with these dates: exemption applications are due on the March 1 taxable status date, the tentative roll comes out May 1, Grievance Day is the fourth Tuesday in May, and the final roll is filed July 1.

There are three levels of review, and each one wants evidence.

  • An informal review with the Assessor, by appointment from October through March, may include an inside and outside inspection.
  • A formal grievance goes to the five-resident Board of Assessment Review on form RP-524. The signed original must arrive with five copies, and faxed or emailed applications are not accepted.
  • Still unhappy after the board rules? File a small claims assessment review petition (RPTL-730) with the Monroe County Clerk, paying $30, no later than 30 days after the final roll.

Bring a recent appraisal, a purchase contract, comparable sales or photos of deferred maintenance. If you plan to sell, a signed listing or purchase offer is also the kind of document the board asks to see.

Property tax and the sale of a Chili house

In Chili, the Receiver of Taxes collects the town and county bill while each school district sends its own. Town and county bills are mailed at the very end of December and should arrive by the end of the first week of January. School bills go out at the very end of August and should arrive by the end of the first week of September. Homeowners with an escrow account get a receipt rather than a bill.

Paying by card at the Chili tax counter or on the town website carries a processing fee. Debit cards have a $3.95 minimum, and credit cards cost 2.45 percent with the same $3.95 minimum. Delinquent taxes owed to the County Treasurer are paid through the Monroe County website, so look at which office the bill names before you pay.

After a sale, the old bill belongs to the new owner. Return it to the Receiver with the new owner's name on it, or forward it directly. A new owner may also face an exemption recapture charge, a one-time amount the Assessor sets when the previous owner had an exemption the buyer does not qualify for. If you carry a senior or disability exemption, tell your buyer before closing so the charge is not a surprise.

Building Department and certificates of occupancy

The Building Department enforces the Chili town code and the New York building codes, and it issues certificates of occupancy or compliance after a final inspection. A project with a permit is not finished until that certificate is issued. Permit applications go through the CloudPermit online system, and the department answers questions about zoning and planning approvals.

Several town rules come up in resale talks.

  • Sheds from 1 to 119 square feet need no permit, sheds from 120 to 196 square feet need a building permit, and sheds of 197 square feet or more need a permit and a variance.
  • Fences need no permit unless the lot is in a flood zone or the fence sits in an easement.
  • Upgrading an electrical panel requires a building permit.
  • Domesticated farm animals, including chickens, need at least 5 acres.
  • The code enforcement officer responds to complaints about rubbish, litter, tall grass and unlicensed vehicles that can be seen from the public right of way.

Closing attorneys often request an instrument survey map. Look through your own closing papers first, then ask the Building Department whether one is on file, and try the Monroe County Clerk after that. If a past project never got a permit, the Building Department can tell you what closing it out takes.

Recording the deed at the Monroe County Clerk

Chili deeds are filed with the Monroe County Clerk, whose office is at 39 W. Main Street, downtown Rochester. A one-page deed costs $50, and every added page is $5. Filing the TP-584 transfer tax return costs $5, the RP-5217 equalization form costs $125 for residential property (and $250 for other property), and each residential deed carries another $10 fee.

The clerk charges transfer tax at $4 per thousand dollars of price. That matches the state rate of $2 for each $500, which the seller pays, and it is due with the TP-584 within 15 days after the deed is delivered. The buyer alone owes the state's 1 percent charge on residences priced at $1 million or more.

The deed must be a dated original with grantor and grantee addresses, a legal description naming the municipality, the new tax number, original signatures and a notary acknowledgment. For same-day recording, be in line by 4:30.

A buyer who pays cash and takes the house as is still goes through this same recording step, so your closing timeline depends on how complete your paperwork is, not on the buyer's financing.

What is the population of Chili, NY?

The 2020 census counted 29,123 people in the town of Chili, up 1.7 percent from 28,625 in 2010. Chili is a Monroe County suburb of Rochester.

When is Grievance Day in Chili?

Every year, on the fourth Tuesday of May. Chili's Board of Assessment Review wants form RP-524 and your evidence in by 8 pm that day.

Which office collects property tax for a Chili house?

The Chili Receiver of Taxes collects the town and county bill at Town Hall, 3333 Chili Avenue. Delinquent taxes go to the Monroe County Treasury, and the school districts send their own bills in September.

Do I need a certificate of occupancy to sell my Chili house?

The town issues a certificate of occupancy or compliance when permitted work passes its final inspection. Work done without a permit can be dealt with before listing if you ask the Building Department what it requires.

What does it cost to record a deed in Monroe County?

Expect $50 for the first deed page and $5 for each more, plus the TP-584 ($5), the RP-5217 ($125 for a residence), a $10 residential fee and transfer tax at $4 per thousand dollars of price.

Selling in Saratoga Springs

The city covers 28.07 square miles in Saratoga County and has a population of 28,768, a 0.9% rise since 2020. Summer race crowds, students and year-round residents all shape demand.

Price is the first question. An owner-occupied home is valued at a median $478,100, about 1.4 times the national $332,700. Your timeline and the house's condition decide this one.

Snowfall averages about 63.5 inches a year here, and January lows sit near 14.3 degrees. Holding a house that needs gutters, a roof or a new boiler through that stretch gets expensive. Ask us for a number and lay it beside a listing estimate.

A cash purchase removes showings, a buyer's mortgage and inspection repair demands. You choose when to close and leave the place as it is.

Property taxes and the equalization rate

The last citywide revaluation was in 2005, no new one is planned, and the current equalization rate is 40%. Assessed values are a fraction of market value, so read a tax bill against that rate and not against the sale price.

  • Rates per $1,000 of assessed value: $7.0973 inside the district and $7.0285 outside, with a county component of $4.562822.
  • Dates: taxable status March 1, tentative roll May 1, final roll July 1.
  • Exemptions: the deadline for all exemptions is March 1.

Basic STAR registrations and Enhanced STAR for seniors go through the state rather than the assessor. Low-income seniors can still apply to the assessor, who needs the federal tax return and a yearly renewal.

The Assessment Office is at 474 Broadway, Suite 14, open 9:00 a.m. to 4:00 p.m. Monday through Friday. Call 518-587-3550, extension 2551. Saratoga County also posts the 2026 tentative and final rolls on its real property tax service page.

Where to pay a city tax bill

Pay online through the finance office's portal, in person at City Hall at 474 Broadway, or by mail to the Commissioner of Finance at PO Box 328. Adirondack Trust Company branches also take payments if you bring the stub. Online payments carry a vendor convenience fee.

Unpaid taxes are usually cleared out of your sale proceeds, so request a payoff figure from the title company early. Even a cash buyer can close with a bill outstanding and settle it the same way.

Historic districts and permits

The city passed a local historic preservation ordinance in 1977, and proposed changes to buildings inside a district go through a review process. Districts include Union Avenue, the Eastside area, Hillside, Broadway and North Broadway, plus one block west of Broadway along streets such as Grand Avenue and Franklin.

If your house falls inside one, ask the Planning Department for the district map and rules. A buyer who plans exterior work will want to know. Outside the districts, the Building Department handles permit applications, status checks and inspection requests, and its counter hours are 9:00 to 12:00 and 1:00 to 4:00.

  • Check whether past exterior changes had review and permits.
  • Request the certificate of occupancy for any converted unit or finished attic.

The Saratoga County Clerk records every deed in the county, with a completed TP-584 and RP-5217 equalization form attached. The clerk offers e-recording through registered facilitators, and a printed copy of your deed costs 50 cents a page in the office.

State transfer tax runs two dollars for every five hundred of price, and any leftover part of a five hundred counts as a full one. The seller pays unless the contract shifts it. A separate 1% mansion tax falls on the buyer once a price hits $1 million.

The county also runs an online real property database where you can pull tax maps and compare sales and assessments, which helps when you price the house.

What to gather before you sell

Anyone who buys will request the same few documents, so collect them now. Begin with your most recent city tax bill and stub, and ask the finance office what is settled. Add the certificate of occupancy for a converted unit or finished attic, plus permit records for exterior work if you are inside a historic district.

Then search your parcel in the county's online real property database, which shows the tax map, your assessment and nearby sales. That gives you an asking price you can defend. Once an offer is accepted, your attorney or title company sends the deed to the County Clerk with the TP-584 and RP-5217.

A clean paper trail makes closing day routine: funds arrive, you sign the deed, taxes and transfer charges come out of proceeds, and the keys change hands. With no lender reviewing the file, a cash buyer can often finish sooner.

If the house needs work

Saratoga Springs shoppers pay for polish. Dated kitchens, worn porches or overdue heating work pull bids down. Repairing everything first means hiring crews, pulling permits and paying carrying costs while the work drags on. Owners who live elsewhere, inherited the place or deal with a tenant often decide that is not worth the trouble.

A direct offer builds the repairs into its number so you leave without a punch list. Weigh it against a listing's net after commissions, carrying costs and repair bills, and get the closing date, buyer's costs and any conditions in writing first.

The last citywide revaluation was in 2005, and the current equalization rate is 40%, so assessments average about 40% of market value. No revaluation is planned. Read your assessment against that rate.
